I was gonna cremate it.') and a final showdown at Crystal Lake. The conflict is sustained through multiple confrontations, chases ('Megan, step out of the car. End of the line.') and violent encounters, making it the dominant structural engine of the film.

title: House
justification: The film's narrative is overwhelmingly driven by conflict, escalating from unsettling dreams and a missing mental patient to a full-blown slasher scenario. The dialogue explicitly introduces a dangerous escaped patient named Robert Henkel, setting up a clear antagonistic force. The characters' actions are primarily dictated by the escalating threat, as evidenced by their attempts to secure the house, call for help, and ultimately fight for survival. The revelation that Beth is connected to the killer as a past victim, Laura, further intensifies the conflict and makes it the central engine of the story, culminating in a violent confrontation and struggle for survival.

title: A Room with a View
justification: Structural conflict is a central engine in "A Room with a View," primarily manifested through social and interpersonal tensions. The initial conflict arises from the inadequate rooms at the pensione, leading to a negotiation with the Emersons ("This is not at all what we were led to expect."). This sets the stage for recurring clashes between different social classes and ideologies, particularly between Lucy's conventional upbringing and the Emersons' unconventional views. Charlotte's disapproval of the Emersons and her attempts to control Lucy's interactions with them create sustained tension ("It would be a serious thing if I were to put her under an obligation...to people of whom I know nothing."). The conflict escalates when Lucy's feelings for George emerge, leading to a confrontation with Charlotte and the breaking of her engagement with Cecil ("Mr. Emerson, go out of this house...and don't come back into it again as long as I live here.").

title: Flight of the Navigator
justification: Structural conflict is a central engine in this narrative. The core conflict arises from David's displacement in time and the subsequent pursuit by NASA, creating sustained antagonism. Explicit threats are present, as NASA seeks to control David and the alien technology, leading to escalating tension. Confrontation is evident in David's repeated escapes and strategic maneuvers to evade capture ("Just take us 20 miles from here"). High-stakes opposition shapes David's decisions, forcing him to choose between family and freedom, culminating in his decision to return to his original time ("If I stay, those scientists will treat me like a guinea pig for the rest of my life").

title: Jo Jo Dancer, Your Life is Calling
justification: The film's narrative is heavily driven by conflict, both internal and external. Jo Jo's struggles with drug addiction, evident in dialogues like "I stopped doing dope. Uh, honest," and his volatile relationships, such as the argument with Michelle culminating in the car crash, "You are one selfish son of a bitch!", create persistent tension. Furthermore, his confrontations with club owners over pay, "I want my motherfucking money," and his strained relationship with his father, "I'll get outta your house! I'm leavin' tonight," contribute to a sustained sense of antagonism. The film also features Jo Jo's internal conflict as he tries to understand his life and mistakes, which is shown through his conversations with himself and others. These conflicts are central to Jo Jo's character arc and drive the plot forward.

title: The Delta Force
justification: The film's narrative is overwhelmingly driven by sustained conflict. The subtitles depict a hijacking, hostage situation, and military rescue operation, all representing escalating antagonism. Explicit threats are constant, such as the hijackers' repeated warnings to blow up the plane if their demands aren't met ("This is a hand grenade, we will blow the plane if you do not do exactly as we say!"). Sustained confrontation is evident in the strategic planning and execution of the Delta Force rescue, as well as the ongoing power struggle between the hijackers and the passengers. The high-stakes opposition shapes character decisions, forcing passengers to make impossible choices (identifying Jewish passengers) and driving the military to risk everything for the rescue.

title: Howard the Duck
justification: Structural conflict is a dominant force in "Howard the Duck." The narrative is propelled by Howard's constant struggle against hostile humans, as evidenced by lines like "Step on him!" and "Shoot to kill!" when he is hunted. This antagonism escalates with the arrival of the Dark Overlord, who explicitly threatens the world's existence: "Tonight the laser beam released me...from that region of demons." Howard's central goal becomes stopping the Overlord, leading to sustained confrontations and high-stakes decisions, such as his choice to destroy the laser despite it being his only way home. The film's progression is heavily reliant on this escalating conflict, making it a central engine of the story.

title: Raw Deal
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The subtitles reveal a sustained antagonism between a former law enforcement officer, Mark, and a powerful crime boss, Patrovita, who is responsible for the death of Mark's son. This fuels Mark's relentless pursuit of revenge and justice, driving the plot forward. Explicit threats and escalating tension are evident in dialogues such as "If you wanna see 'em again, meet me" and scenes of violence, like the attacks on Lamanski and the police stations. The high-stakes opposition shapes Mark's decisions, leading him to infiltrate Patrovita's organization and engage in strategic confrontations, making conflict the central element of the story.

title: Armed and Dangerous
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The film revolves around Frank Dooley's pursuit of justice after being framed for corruption, leading him and his partner Norman Kane into direct opposition with Michael Carlino's criminal enterprise. This antagonism escalates throughout the film, featuring explicit threats ('If I go to jail, I'll kill you'), escalating tension (the armored car heist), and sustained confrontation (the final showdown with Carlino). The high stakes of the conflict, involving union racketeering, grand theft, and murder, directly shape the characters' decisions and drive nearly all narrative progression, making conflict the central structural element.

title: Legend
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The subtitles establish a clear and persistent antagonism between the Lord of Darkness and forces of light, primarily represented by the unicorns. The Lord of Darkness explicitly states his goal to eliminate the unicorns and plunge the world into eternal night, creating a high-stakes opposition that drives the plot. The goblins, led by Blix, are tasked with hunting and killing the unicorns, leading to direct confrontations and escalating tension. The narrative revolves around the characters' attempts to thwart the Lord of Darkness's plans and restore balance, making conflict the central element.

title: Song of the South
justification: Structural conflict is central to the narrative. The film opens with the conflict of Johnny's parents' separation and his father's departure, which drives Johnny to run away. This initial conflict is compounded by Johnny's struggles to adjust to his new life and his interactions with the Favers boys, who antagonize him and threaten his puppy, Teenchy. Uncle Remus's stories, while seemingly lighthearted, often revolve around conflict between Brer Rabbit and Brer Fox, mirroring Johnny's own struggles. The climax involves Johnny's accident while trying to prevent Uncle Remus from leaving, highlighting the emotional stakes and the central role of conflict in shaping the narrative's progression and resolution.

title: The Morning After
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The subtitles reveal a sustained and escalating conflict centered around Viveca, who is framed for murder. The narrative is driven by her attempts to prove her innocence while evading the police and uncovering the real killer. This is evident in the dialogue where Viveca seeks help from Jacky and Turner, constantly discussing the body, the setup, and the need to stay ahead of the authorities. The subtitles reveal a sustained antagonism between RoboCop and criminal elements, particularly Clarence Boddicker's gang, with escalating violence and explicit threats ('Dead or alive, you're coming with me'). A major conflict arises between RoboCop and OCP, specifically Dick Jones, due to Directive 4, which prevents RoboCop from arresting senior OCP officers, creating a high-stakes opposition. The police strike further escalates the conflict, highlighting the city's descent into chaos and the power struggle between OCP and law enforcement. The narrative is almost entirely driven by these sustained conflicts and threats.

title: Outrageous Fortune
justification: The film's narrative is overwhelmingly driven by conflict. Initially, the conflict is interpersonal, with rivalries between actresses and romantic tensions. However, this quickly escalates into a high-stakes espionage plot involving a stolen virus. The protagonists are pursued by both Russian and American agents, creating constant threat and danger. Dialogue such as "They're looking for Michael," "We gotta get back on the trail," and explicit threats like "I'm gonna break every bone in your body!" demonstrate the escalating tension and sustained antagonism. The protagonists' decisions are consistently shaped by the need to survive and retrieve the virus, making conflict the dominant engine of the story.

title: The Living Daylights
justification: Structural conflict is a dominant force in this narrative. The film revolves around the defection of General Koskov and the subsequent investigation into a potential assassination plot (Smiert Spionom) orchestrated by General Pushkin. This creates persistent antagonism between Bond and the perceived threat of Pushkin, driving Bond's actions and decisions. The escalating tension is evident in the numerous confrontations, including the initial sniper incident, the safe house attack, and the eventual showdown with Whitaker. The high stakes are clear: preventing a war between the Soviet Union and the West.

title: Full Metal Jacket
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film. The first half centers on the brutal antagonism between Gunnery Sergeant Hartman and his recruits, particularly Private Pyle, with escalating tension and threats. Hartman's dialogue is filled with insults and punishments: "I will PT you all until you fucking die!" and "I will gouge out your eyeballs and skull-fuck you!" The second half shifts to the Vietnam War, where the central conflict is the Marines versus the Viet Cong. This is evident in the dialogue: "The NVA are dug in deep" and "We're getting killed for these people, and they don't even appreciate it." The film culminates in a sustained confrontation with a sniper, resulting in casualties and shaping character decisions.

title: A Nightmare On Elm Street 3: Dream Warriors
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The subtitles reveal a sustained and escalating conflict between the protagonists (Kristen, Nancy, and the other teens) and Freddy Krueger, a supernatural antagonist. This conflict is explicitly framed as a battle for survival against a malevolent force that invades their dreams, with the threat of death being constant. The dialogue emphasizes the high stakes, as characters strategize and confront Freddy directly in the dream world. The narrative progresses almost entirely through confrontations with Freddy, attempts to understand his origins, and efforts to protect themselves and each other from his attacks, making conflict the central driving force.

title: Blind Date
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of this film's narrative. The subtitles reveal persistent antagonism, escalating tension, and sustained confrontation throughout the story. Nadia is being chased by her psychotic ex-boyfriend David, who repeatedly threatens Walter. Walter's professional life is also in conflict, as he is fired from his job. The narrative culminates in a courtroom drama and a chaotic wedding, both driven by the central conflict between Nadia, David, and Walter, with high stakes and significant consequences for all involved.

title: Roxanne
justification: Structural conflict is a central element in "Roxanne." The film revolves around C.D.'s internal conflict regarding his appearance and his external conflict with Chris over Roxanne's affections. C.D. struggles with his self-esteem due to his large nose, leading to avoidance and insecurity in romantic pursuits, as evidenced by his reluctance to directly express his feelings to Roxanne. The rivalry between C.D. and Chris escalates as C.D. ghostwrites letters and dialogue for Chris, creating a deceptive dynamic that ultimately leads to confrontation and emotional turmoil. The tension builds as Roxanne becomes increasingly enamored with the false persona, culminating in a dramatic reveal and a final showdown where C.D. must overcome his insecurities to win her over.

title: Planes, Trains & Automobiles
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The entire plot revolves around Neal's desperate attempt to get home for Thanksgiving, constantly thwarted by escalating conflicts and antagonisms. These conflicts range from the initial cab theft and airline mishaps to the ongoing clashes with Del, who becomes both a source of and a solution to Neal's problems. The stakes are high, as Neal repeatedly emphasizes his family's expectations and his desire to be home. The film's progression is almost entirely driven by these sustained confrontations and escalating threats to Neal's journey, making conflict the central structural element.

title: Spaceballs
justification: The film's narrative is overwhelmingly driven by conflict. Spaceballs, led by Dark Helmet and President Skroob, are in constant antagonism with Planet Druidia, seeking to steal their air. This antagonism manifests as direct threats ('Once we kidnap the princess, her father'll give us the combination to the air shield, thereby destroying Planet Druidia'), escalating tension (laser battles, chases), and sustained confrontation (kidnapping attempts, rescue missions). The high stakes (the destruction of a planet) shape character decisions, particularly Lone Starr's and Princess Vespa's, making conflict the central engine of the story. The subtitles are replete with examples of this sustained conflict, from the initial pursuit of Princess Vespa to the final showdown on Spaceball One.

title: Mannequin
justification: Structural conflict is a central element in this narrative. The primary conflict revolves around the potential sale of Prince and Company to Illustra, a corporation seeking to demolish the store. This is evident in dialogues such as "It's like a ghost ship around here. They're gonna be begging to sell this place within a month." and "We'll build the best Illustra yet on that site." Jonathan's creative window displays are a direct challenge to Illustra's plans, creating tension and driving the plot forward. Additionally, Jonathan faces recurring conflicts with authority figures like Mr. Richards, who actively tries to undermine him, and the constant threat of losing his job, as seen in multiple instances of him being fired and rehired.

title: Eddie Murphy Raw
justification: The monologue is structured around conflict, primarily through the comedian's anecdotes about confrontations and disagreements. He recounts his fear of Mr. T wanting to "whip Eddie Murphy's ass," and his imagined confrontation with Michael Jackson. A significant portion of the monologue details his contentious phone call with Bill Cosby, highlighting their differing views on comedy. He also describes a physical altercation he had with an Italian man, emphasizing the escalating tension and eventual fight. These recurring narratives of conflict and potential conflict drive the comedic structure and provide the core material for his performance.

title: Throw Momma From the Train
justification: Structural conflict is a central engine of the narrative. The film revolves around Larry's intense conflict with his ex-wife, Margaret, who stole his book and achieved success. This antagonism is evident from the beginning, with Larry's outbursts about Margaret's success and his desire to 'get it back.' The introduction of Owen escalates the conflict, as he misinterprets Larry's expressions of hatred and takes it upon himself to murder Margaret, leading to a 'crisscross' murder plot. This creates a sustained threat and escalating tension, as Larry is now implicated in a crime he didn't commit and must deal with Owen's increasingly erratic behavior and the police investigation.

title: The Running Man
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The central conflict revolves around Ben Richards, framed as a mass murderer, being forced to participate in a deadly game show called "The Running Man," where he is hunted by various stalkers. This is evident from the dialogue: "Eliminate anything moving," "All rioters must be eliminated," and Killian's repeated emphasis on the show's violence and high stakes. Richards's struggle for survival against the stalkers and the corrupt network forms the core of the plot, with escalating tension and physical confrontations driving the narrative forward. The conflict is sustained throughout the film, shaping character decisions and dictating the progression of events, as Richards and his allies attempt to expose the truth and overthrow the oppressive regime.

title: No Way Out
justification: The film's narrative is overwhelmingly driven by conflict. The central plot revolves around a murder investigation that quickly escalates into a high-stakes cover-up involving the Secretary of Defense and a potential Soviet spy. Dialogue reveals persistent antagonism between characters, such as the power struggles between the Secretary of Defense, Senator Duvall, and the CIA director. Explicit threats and escalating tension are evident as the investigation progresses, with characters like Tom Farrell facing increasing danger and pressure to conform. The sustained confrontation between Farrell, Pritchard, and Brice, along with the constant threat of exposure, makes conflict the dominant engine of the story.

title: Summer School
justification: Structural conflict is a central engine driving the narrative. The primary conflict arises from the threat of summer school, which motivates the students and Shoop. This is immediately established when the students learn they failed their English test and must attend summer school, prompting Shoop to gamble to avoid it. However, he is blackmailed into teaching summer school, creating a conflict between his desire for a vacation and his need for tenure. The conflict escalates as Shoop struggles to control his unruly students, facing suspension and pressure from Gills, who actively antagonizes him. The students' initial resistance to learning and Shoop's unconventional teaching methods further fuel the conflict, culminating in their need to pass the skills test to save his job.

title: Like Father Like Son
justification: Structural conflict is a central engine in this narrative, primarily through the antagonism between Dr. Jack Hammond and Dr. Armbruster for the Chief of Staff position. This is evident in dialogues like, "Dear, I hope you're going to take my advice and make Jack the next Chief of Staff," and "I'm supporting someone else for Chief of Staff." Additionally, Chris's academic struggles and his father's intense pressure create internal conflict, as seen in "Hammonds just don't get 'Cs'." Rick's persistent bullying of Chris, escalating into physical altercations, further contributes to the film's structural conflict, exemplified by "You better watch your step, dickhead." The conflict surrounding indigent care, highlighted by Dr. Larkin's advocacy and the board's resistance, also shapes the narrative, as shown in "You've got people out there who are sick and dying, and their only sin is that they don't have the money to get in here."

title: Adventures in Babysitting
justification: The film's narrative is almost entirely driven by escalating conflict. Chris's babysitting job quickly spirals out of control, initiating a series of escalating confrontations. These include evading car thieves ("What are you doing here? My wife called the cops."), navigating gang warfare ("So as soon as we cross Devereaux street, you and your girls is dead meat."), and escaping from criminals who want a magazine ("Give me the magazine and get out of here."). The central plot revolves around Chris and the children's struggle to survive these dangerous situations and return home safely, making conflict the dominant engine of the story.

title: The Lost Boys
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The central conflict revolves around the threat of vampirism and the fight against vampires in Santa Carla. This is evident from dialogues such as: "You're a vampire, Michael!" and "Santa Carla is crawling with vampires." The escalating tension is sustained through explicit threats and confrontations, such as the vampire gang's attempts to turn Michael and the Frog brothers' vampire hunting activities. The high stakes are clear: "If you kill the head vampire...all half-vampires will return to normal," driving the characters' decisions and actions throughout the film. The narrative progresses almost entirely through sustained antagonism between the protagonists and the vampires, making conflict the primary structural element.

title: Wall Street
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The central conflict revolves around Bud Fox's ambition and his relationship with Gordon Gekko, which escalates into a high-stakes battle involving insider trading, corporate raiding, and ethical compromises. Gekko's predatory business practices and Bud's internal struggle between loyalty and morality drive the plot forward, creating persistent antagonism. Explicit threats and escalating tension are evident in dialogues such as Gekko's instructions to "rip their fucking throats out" and his assertion that "money never sleeps." The sustained confrontation between Gekko and Wildman, as well as Bud's eventual betrayal of Gekko, further underscore the centrality of conflict to the narrative structure.

title: Can’t Buy Me Love
justification: Structural conflict is a central engine in this film. The narrative revolves around Ronald's desire to become popular, leading him to pay Cindy to feign a relationship. This arrangement creates sustained antagonism, as evidenced by Cindy's initial reluctance and the social repercussions they both face. The dialogue highlights escalating tension, such as when Cindy says, "For one month you draped all over me like a cheap Fucking Suit!" and the subsequent fallout at the party where their arrangement is exposed. The film's climax involves a confrontation where Ronald's actions are revealed, leading to social ostracization and the need for reconciliation, solidifying conflict as a major driver of the plot.

title: The Princess Bride
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The central plot revolves around Buttercup's kidnapping, which initiates a series of escalating confrontations. Westley faces constant opposition, battling Vizzini's henchmen (Inigo, Fezzik), navigating the Fire Swamp, and ultimately confronting Prince Humperdinck. Inigo seeks revenge for his father's murder, leading to a sustained duel with Count Rugen. The Prince's scheme to start a war with Guilder adds another layer of strategic conflict, with Buttercup as a pawn. The narrative is propelled forward almost entirely by these antagonistic forces and the high stakes involved.

title: Harry and the Hendersons
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The central conflict revolves around the Henderson family's accidental encounter with Bigfoot, whom they name Harry. This initial conflict escalates as they try to conceal Harry's existence from the outside world, particularly from authorities and a determined hunter, LaFleur. The family faces persistent threats of discovery, leading to sustained confrontations and high-stakes decisions, such as whether to protect Harry or turn him in. The dialogue highlights this tension, with characters repeatedly expressing fear of exposure and LaFleur's relentless pursuit, making conflict the primary driver of the plot.

title: Police Academy 4: Citizens on Patrol
justification: Structural conflict is a central engine in this narrative. The primary conflict stems from Captain Harris's overt opposition to Commandant Lassard's C.O.P. program, as evidenced by his statement, "Lassard's program is a mistake...and anyone who thinks otherwise is wrong." This antagonism drives much of the plot, with Harris actively sabotaging the program and clashing with Mahoney, who supports it. Further conflict arises from the escaped criminals, requiring the C.O.P. members and police to engage in pursuit and confrontation, escalating the stakes. The film culminates in a large-scale chase and capture, solidifying conflict as a dominant structural element.

title: Tin Men
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The central conflict revolves around the escalating antagonism between Tilley and Babowsky, beginning with a car accident and escalating into a series of retaliatory acts. Dialogue such as "I'm gonna get even with you" and "You're dead! Dead! Dead!" explicitly establishes the sustained threat and escalating tension. This conflict shapes character decisions, such as Tilley's obsession with revenge and Babowsky's attempts to evade him. The narrative progresses primarily through their confrontations, making conflict the central structural element.

title: Black Widow
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The central conflict revolves around Alex Barnes's relentless pursuit of a suspected serial killer, a woman who marries wealthy men and then poisons them. This pursuit is evident from the beginning, with Alex investigating suspicious deaths and uncovering a pattern. The escalating tension is sustained through dialogue revealing new victims, potential suspects, and the challenges Alex faces in proving her theory. The narrative is driven by Alex's strategic confrontations with her superiors, potential victims, and ultimately, the killer herself, making conflict the primary force behind the plot's progression.

title: Broadcast News
justification: Structural conflict is a central engine in this film, primarily manifested through professional rivalries and ethical dilemmas within the news broadcasting industry. The tension between characters like Jane, Aaron, and Tom, vying for success and recognition, creates persistent antagonism. Explicit threats to job security due to budget cuts and layoffs escalate the tension. Sustained confrontation arises from differing journalistic ethics, such as staging news or prioritizing entertainment over substance, shaping character decisions and driving the narrative forward, especially concerning Jane's career choices and relationships.

title: Nuts
justification: Structural conflict is a dominant force in this film, primarily revolving around Claudia Kirk's legal battle and her competency to stand trial for manslaughter. The narrative is driven by the antagonism between the prosecution, seeking to prove her guilt or incompetence ("THE DEFENDANT IS CHARGED WITH MANSLAUGHTER"), and the defense, initially attempting to have her committed to a mental facility, then later fighting for her right to stand trial. This is evident in the courtroom scenes, where opposing lawyers clash ("I MOVE TO CONTROVERT," "WHAT'S YOUR BASIS, LEVINSKY?"). The high stakes of the trial, with Claudia facing a lengthy prison sentence or indefinite commitment, shape character decisions and drive the plot forward. The conflict escalates with dramatic courtroom outbursts and challenges to witness testimonies, making it a central engine of the story.

title: *batteries not included
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The subtitles reveal a sustained and escalating conflict between the tenants of a building and developers trying to force them out. This conflict is explicitly stated through dialogue like "They're paying you to move out" and "You take the money and move out, OK?" The conflict escalates to physical violence, threats, and intimidation, as seen in lines such as "Get out of my place, you punks!" and "There, now you got less to move." The high stakes of losing their homes and the persistent antagonism drive the characters' decisions and actions throughout the film, making conflict the central organizing principle.

title: Baby Boom
justification: Structural conflict is a central theme in this film. J.C. Wiatt, a high-powered executive, faces persistent antagonism in both her professional and personal life. Initially, the conflict is career-driven, with J.C. battling for partnership and dealing with corporate power struggles, as evidenced by her interactions with Fritz and Ken. The introduction of Elizabeth creates a new arena of conflict, forcing J.C. to confront her identity and priorities. This is highlighted by her struggle to balance work and childcare, culminating in her decision to reject a lucrative offer from The Food Chain to maintain her newfound family life in Vermont.

title: Ernest Goes to Camp
justification: The film's narrative is heavily driven by conflict. Initially, there's tension between Ernest and his desire to be a counselor versus his actual capabilities. This is superseded by the central conflict: the struggle to save Kamp Kikakee from the mining company. This conflict escalates throughout the film, featuring explicit threats ('We'll have no choice. We'll have to send them back'), sustained confrontation (the boys fighting the other campers, then the miners), and high stakes (losing the camp, going back to the institution). The climax involves a full-blown battle to prevent the destruction of the camp, making conflict the dominant engine of the story.

title: Raising Arizona
justification: Structural conflict is a dominant force in "Raising Arizona." The central plot revolves around Hi and Ed's decision to kidnap Nathan Junior, immediately establishing a high-stakes conflict with the Arizona family and the law. This act triggers escalating tension as they evade authorities, including the relentless manhunter Leonard Smalls, who poses a constant threat. The conflict is further amplified by the presence of Gale and Evelle, escaped convicts who complicate Hi and Ed's plans and introduce additional layers of danger and antagonism. The narrative is propelled by these sustained confrontations and threats, shaping the characters' decisions and driving the story forward, as evidenced by the constant pursuit and the escalating stakes of their actions.

title: Revenge of the Nerds II: Nerds in Paradise
justification: The film's narrative is heavily structured around the conflict between the Tri-Lambs and the Alpha Betas. This antagonism is established early when the Tri-Lambs are denied rooms at the Royal Flamingo due to Buzz Mussinger's prejudice. The conflict escalates with pranks, sabotage, and attempts to expel the Tri-Lambs from the United Fraternity Conference, as evidenced by Roger Lattimore's schemes and Proposition 15. The Tri-Lambs' struggle to overcome these obstacles and assert their right to participate in the conference drives the plot forward, culminating in a final confrontation and resolution. The dialogue consistently highlights the animosity and strategic maneuvering between the two groups, making conflict the central engine of the story.

title: Jaws 4: The Revenge
justification: Structural conflict is a central engine in this narrative. The film revolves around Ellen Brody's fear of the ocean and her belief that a shark is intentionally targeting her family, creating persistent antagonism. This is evident in her repeated demands for her son Michael to quit his job, stating, "I don't want my family anywhere near the water again. Never!" The escalating tension is further fueled by the shark attacks, including the death of Sean and the attack on Thea, which drive the plot forward. The sustained confrontation between the Brody family and the perceived threat of the shark culminates in a high-stakes showdown at sea, where they actively hunt and attempt to destroy the creature, shaping their decisions and actions throughout the film.

title: Hello Again
justification: Structural conflict is a central engine in this narrative. The film revolves around Lucy's death and subsequent return, which immediately creates antagonism. Lucy's return disrupts Jason's new life with Kim, leading to sustained confrontation and escalating tension as Kim tries to discredit Lucy. The conflict is further heightened by the threat of Lucy disappearing again if she doesn't find true love, shaping her decisions and driving the plot. The narrative is propelled by the opposition between Lucy and Kim, as well as Lucy's struggle to reclaim her life and find her place in a world that has moved on without her.

title: Critical Condition
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of this film's narrative. The central character, Lennihan, is immediately embroiled in conflict with a loan shark, Palazzi, and then with the police after being set up. This initial conflict escalates as Lennihan is sentenced to prison, where he faces threats from Harris. The narrative then shifts to the insane asylum, where Lennihan instigates a strike and ultimately a riot, leading to conflict with hospital staff and other patients. The hurricane and subsequent power outage exacerbate the chaos, creating further conflict as Lennihan impersonates a doctor and navigates the escalating crisis. The film culminates in a violent confrontation with Stucky and Chambers, solidifying conflict as the primary driver of the plot.

title: Innerspace
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the narrative. The film is driven by the antagonism between the protagonists (Tuck and Jack) and the antagonists (Scrimshaw, Igoe, and Canker) who are after the stolen microchip and Tuck. This is evident from the moment Tuck is miniaturized and accidentally injected into Jack, setting off a chain of escalating threats and confrontations. The dialogue highlights the urgency of Tuck's situation ('my air supply is running out') and the antagonists' relentless pursuit ('We need that syringe'). The conflict escalates into physical altercations, chases, and strategic maneuvers, with the protagonists constantly evading capture and fighting to survive. The high stakes are clear: Tuck's life and the control of miniaturization technology are on the line, shaping every decision made by the characters.

title: Overboard
justification: Structural conflict is a central engine driving the narrative. The film is initiated by a sustained antagonism between Joanna and Dean, escalating from a dispute over carpentry work to Dean's elaborate revenge plot involving amnesia and forced domestic servitude. This central conflict shapes the majority of the plot, as Joanna struggles to adapt to her new life and Dean attempts to maintain the deception. The conflict is further heightened by the threat of Joanna regaining her memory and the potential consequences for Dean. The narrative progresses through a series of confrontations, both physical and psychological, as Joanna resists her imposed role and Dean tries to control the situation, making conflict a dominant structural element.

title: The Principal
justification: The film's narrative is overwhelmingly driven by conflict. Rick Latimer's arrival at Brandel High immediately plunges him into a sustained battle against gang violence, drug dealing, and student intimidation, primarily orchestrated by Victor Duncan. This conflict escalates throughout the film, with explicit threats made against Latimer ('You're a dead man if you come here tomorrow'), physical confrontations ('Break it up!'), and strategic maneuvering as Latimer attempts to enforce his 'No more' policy. The conflict shapes nearly every major development, from Latimer's attempts to reform the school to his personal relationships, making it the dominant structural engine of the film.

title: Suspect
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The central conflict revolves around the murder of Elizabeth Quinn and the subsequent trial of Carl Anderson, with the narrative heavily focused on the adversarial legal proceedings and the search for the true killer. The subtitles reveal escalating tension as Kathleen Riley, the public defender, uncovers a conspiracy involving high-ranking officials, including a judge and the Deputy Attorney General, who are implicated in the murder and a past case-fixing scandal. The narrative is driven by Riley's sustained confrontation with these powerful figures, as evidenced by her courtroom showdowns and investigative efforts, creating a high-stakes opposition that shapes character decisions and propels the story forward. The explicit threats and danger Riley faces as she gets closer to the truth further emphasize the centrality of conflict to the narrative structure.

title: The Believers
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The subtitles reveal a sustained antagonism between Cal, the protagonist, and a cult led by Dennis and Calder, who seek to sacrifice Cal's son, Chris. This conflict escalates throughout the film, with explicit threats to Chris's safety, as evidenced by Lopez's warnings ('You're in danger. You and your son. Hurry.') and Carmen's attempts to protect him ('He's in danger! I'm trying to protect him!'). The narrative is driven by Cal's efforts to understand and thwart the cult's plans, leading to a final confrontation where he must save Chris from being sacrificed ('It is God's will that innocence redeem the world.').

title: Some Kind of Wonderful
justification: Structural conflict is a central engine driving the narrative. The film revolves around Keith's romantic pursuit of Amanda, which is fraught with antagonism from her ex-boyfriend, Hardy, and his social circle. This conflict escalates throughout the film, culminating in a physical confrontation. Dialogue such as Hardy's threats ("capable of reducing your head to a crimson stain on the wall") and Laura's warning ("She's only going out with you so she can get you to Hardy Jenns's house... so he can mess you up") highlight the escalating tension and danger. Keith's decision to confront Hardy despite the risks demonstrates how the conflict shapes his actions and the narrative's progression.

title: Project X
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The central conflict revolves around the ethical implications of the Air Force's experimental program using chimpanzees, specifically Virgil, for radiation testing. This is evident in the dialogue where Teri fights to prevent Virgil from being used in the experiments ('They're not taking Virgil away.') and Jimmy grapples with the moral implications of his role ('Are they all...? Yes, all.'). The escalating tension culminates in Jimmy and Teri's decision to steal an airplane to free the chimpanzees, leading to a chase and crash ('We have a runaway aircraft heading down Taxiway 3.'). The narrative is almost entirely driven by this sustained antagonism between those seeking to exploit the chimps and those trying to protect them.

title: The Big Easy
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the narrative. The film revolves around a series of escalating conflicts, primarily a drug war between Vinnie "The Cannon" Di Moti's Italian-American gang and Daddy Mention's black narcotics operation, triggered by the murder of Freddy Angelo. This conflict is further complicated by police corruption, as evidenced by Lieutenant Remy McSwain's investigation into the Angelo murder and the subsequent exposure of Captain Kellom's involvement in the drug trade. The escalating violence, betrayals, and high-stakes confrontations drive the plot forward, shaping character decisions and narrative progression. The subtitles are replete with dialogue indicating persistent antagonism, explicit threats, and sustained confrontation, making conflict the central structural element.

title: Born in East L.A.
justification: Structural conflict is a central engine driving the narrative. The film's plot is initiated by Rudy's accidental deportation to Mexico, setting up an immediate antagonistic situation against his will ("I'm an American citizen, I demand to see my..."). This conflict escalates as he faces exploitation and danger in Tijuana, struggling to return home ("All I wanna do is get back home"). Rudy's journey is marked by recurring confrontations with border patrol, criminals, and cultural barriers, all of which directly impede his goal and shape his decisions. The sustained opposition and escalating stakes make conflict a dominant structural element.

title: Masters of the Universe
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The subtitles establish a clear and persistent antagonism between He-Man and Skeletor, with the latter's explicit goal to capture Castle Grayskull and become 'masters of the universe.' This conflict escalates rapidly with Skeletor's initial victory, imprisonment of the Sorceress, and declaration of war against Eternia. The rest of the film is driven by He-Man's efforts to thwart Skeletor, retrieve the Cosmic Key, and save the Sorceress, with recurring confrontations and escalating stakes. The dialogue is saturated with threats, strategic planning, and descriptions of ongoing battles, making conflict the central element shaping character decisions and narrative progression.

title: Angel Heart
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The entire plot revolves around Harry Angel's search for Johnny Favorite, which is fraught with escalating tension and danger. This search leads to a series of murders, making Harry a suspect and placing him in direct conflict with both the police and the mysterious Louis Cyphre. The high stakes of the investigation, coupled with the constant threat of violence and the supernatural elements, drive Harry's decisions and actions, making conflict the central element of the story. The dialogue reveals a persistent antagonism and escalating tension, culminating in the revelation of Harry's true identity and his inescapable fate.

title: Empire of the Sun
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The initial conflict arises from the growing tensions between Japan and other nations, escalating into war, which separates Jamie from his parents. This separation and the struggle for survival in Japanese-occupied Shanghai and internment camps drive the plot. Jamie faces constant threats of violence, starvation, and disease, forcing him into strategic alliances and desperate decisions. The film culminates with the atomic bombing and the struggle for liberation, highlighting the pervasive and sustained antagonism that shapes Jamie's journey.

title: Burglar
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The subtitles reveal a sustained series of escalating conflicts: a planned burglary gone wrong, leading to murder accusations, police pursuit, and double-crosses. The protagonist, Bernie, is constantly threatened by Ray, a corrupt cop demanding money ("I want $20,000 payable today right now"), and is forced to commit further crimes to survive. The narrative is driven by the need to clear his name and evade capture, as evidenced by lines like "Tomorrow they're going to haul my black ass back to jail, probably for murder now." The film culminates in a violent confrontation and chase, solidifying conflict as the central structural element.

title: Over the Top
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The central conflict revolves around Lincoln Hawk's struggle to reconnect with his estranged son, Michael, while simultaneously battling his overbearing father-in-law, Jason Cutler, for custody. This antagonism is evident from the outset, with Cutler's disapproval and attempts to undermine Hawk's relationship with Michael: "I didn't fly all the way up here to be simply told you turned my grandson over to that worthless bastard!" The escalating tension is further fueled by Cutler's attempts to sabotage Hawk, including hiring thugs to attack him and Michael: "Why are you doing this? Shut up!" The high-stakes arm-wrestling competition serves as a physical manifestation of Hawk's struggle for redemption and his son's affection, with the outcome directly impacting their future together. The narrative is almost entirely driven by these sustained conflicts.

title: Benji the Hunted
justification: The narrative is structured around the conflict of Benji being lost at sea and the search to find him. The news report details the capsized boat and the missing dog, establishing the central problem. The dialogue with Frank Inn highlights the immediate aftermath of the accident and the uncertainty surrounding Benji's fate. Additionally, there's a separate, minor conflict introduced with the man who is being pursued for a reward, though its connection to the main plot is unclear from the provided subtitles. The search for Benji and the pursuit of the man create tension and drive the immediate narrative forward, though other themes may also be present.

title: Radio Days
justification: Structural conflict is a central engine in this film, though not the only one. The narrative is driven by various forms of antagonism and tension. The most prominent is World War II, which casts a long shadow over the characters' lives, influencing their fears, hopes, and daily routines ("Between the Nazis and the Communists, give me those Reds."). Family conflicts are also recurring, such as the constant bickering between the narrator's parents and the tensions within the extended family ("two people who could find an argument in any subject"). Aunt Bea's desperate search for love and the challenges she faces also contribute to the film's structural conflict, as does the cultural clash between traditional Jewish values and modern ideologies, exemplified by the conflict with the communist neighbors during Yom Kippur ("They're Jewish... but they don't believe in God, just Stalin.").

title: Hellraiser
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The subtitles reveal a sustained antagonism between Kirsty and the resurrected Frank, who requires blood to regenerate. This conflict escalates as Frank manipulates Julia into providing him with victims, creating a recurring threat to those around them. The Cenobites' pursuit of Frank, and later Kirsty, adds another layer of escalating tension and danger. Kirsty's strategic attempts to outwit Frank and the Cenobites, culminating in a final confrontation, demonstrate how conflict shapes character decisions and drives the narrative forward.

title: Superman IV: The Quest for Peace
justification: Structural conflict is a dominant force in this film. The narrative revolves around Superman's struggle against Lex Luthor and his creation, Nuclear Man. Luthor's explicit goal is to 'Destroy Superman!' and he actively schemes to achieve this, creating escalating tension. Superman faces constant threats and must make high-stakes decisions to protect Earth, as evidenced by his choice to remove all nuclear weapons, which is met with resistance and further conflict. The film's progression is largely driven by this sustained antagonism.

title: The Aristocats
justification: Structural conflict is a central engine driving the narrative of *The Aristocats*. The primary conflict arises from Edgar's plot to eliminate Duchess and her kittens to inherit Madame Adelaide's fortune, as revealed through dialogue like, "Those cats have got to go" and "I'll think of a way." This antagonism initiates a series of escalating threats and confrontations, including Edgar drugging the cats and abandoning them in the countryside. The cats' journey back to Paris is fraught with danger, including encounters with aggressive dogs ("Nice doggy, nice doggy. Heel, roll over, play dead!") and near-drowning experiences, all directly stemming from Edgar's initial act of aggression. The climax involves a sustained confrontation between Edgar and the alley cats, who intervene to save Duchess and her kittens, solidifying conflict as a dominant structural element.

title: Ishtar
justification: Structural conflict is a central theme, primarily driven by political intrigue and survival. The narrative escalates quickly when Chuck and Lyle inadvertently become entangled in a Middle Eastern power struggle after Chuck exchanges passports with Shirra Assel, a wanted revolutionary. This act places them in direct opposition to the CIA and the Emir's forces, leading to escalating threats and attempts on their lives: "A little while ago, your men tried to kill two Americans in Marrakech." The conflict intensifies as they are pursued through the desert, culminating in a violent confrontation with a helicopter and armed forces: "They're splitting. Go for the one in blue." The high stakes and persistent antagonism significantly shape the characters' decisions and drive the plot forward, although comedic elements temper the overall intensity.

title: The Mission
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The subtitles reveal persistent antagonism between the Jesuit missions and colonial powers (Spanish and Portuguese settlers), driven by competing interests over land and indigenous labor. Explicit threats and escalating tension are evident in dialogues concerning slavery, territorial disputes, and the impending transfer of mission territories. Sustained confrontation occurs on multiple levels: physical (armed conflict), psychological (Mendoza's internal struggle and the Cardinal's moral dilemma), strategic (political maneuvering by the church and colonial authorities), and institutional (Jesuits vs. colonial administration). The high-stakes opposition shapes character decisions, particularly regarding resistance versus obedience, culminating in a violent climax. The narrative progresses almost entirely through this sustained conflict, making it the central structural element.

title: Prince of Darkness
justification: The film's narrative is overwhelmingly driven by conflict. The central plot revolves around the discovery and attempted containment of an ancient evil force, immediately establishing a high-stakes antagonistic relationship. The dialogue is replete with escalating threats, as characters grapple with the growing power of the entity and its influence on others ('He's gaining strength. I can feel it all around us now.'). Sustained confrontation is evident in the characters' desperate attempts to understand and combat the evil, leading to violent struggles and strategic decisions aimed at survival ('We stopped it here. Through the grace of God... I stopped it.'). The film culminates in a final, desperate battle against the entity, solidifying conflict as the dominant structural engine.

title: Flowers in the Attic
justification: The narrative is overwhelmingly driven by conflict. The central conflict is between the children and their grandmother, who imprisons and abuses them. This is compounded by the mother's betrayal, prioritizing inheritance over her children's well-being, creating a sustained antagonism. The children face constant threats of punishment, starvation, and exposure, escalating the tension. Their decisions are shaped by the need to survive and escape, making conflict the dominant engine of the story.

title: Creepshow 2
justification: The film's narrative is significantly driven by conflict, though not exclusively. The first segment, "Old Chief Wood'nhead," features escalating tension as Sam Whitemoon and his gang threaten and ultimately rob Ray and Martha, leading to Martha's death and Ray's vengeful actions. This sustained antagonism shapes the story's progression. "The Raft" presents a different kind of conflict: survival against an unknown, deadly entity. The characters are in constant danger, and their decisions are dictated by the need to avoid the creature. Finally, "The Hitch-Hiker" revolves around Annie's escalating psychological conflict after a hit-and-run, haunted by the victim's persistent presence.

title: Hamburger Hill
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The subtitles are saturated with explicit antagonism, escalating tension, and sustained confrontation. The dialogue is filled with the realities of war, including incoming fire ("What did they say that signal for incoming rounds was?"), ground attacks ("What's the signal for ground attack?"), and the ever-present threat of the enemy ("Han is going to cut your fucking throat"). The film revolves around the repeated attempts to take a heavily defended hill, resulting in constant combat and casualties ("We've been up and down this hill... nine fucking times."). The high stakes of survival in a war zone shape nearly every character decision and interaction, making conflict the central driving force.

title: The Pick-Up Artist
justification: Structural conflict is a central engine driving the narrative. The film revolves around Jack Jericho's interactions with various women, but these encounters are frequently complicated by external threats and escalating tension. For example, Lulu is entangled with a dangerous boyfriend, Alonzo, leading to threats and physical confrontations. Randy is in debt to gangsters, creating a high-stakes situation that forces Jack to intervene. The dialogue explicitly reveals these conflicts, such as Alonzo's threats to Lulu and the gangsters' demands for money from Randy's father, Flash. These conflicts shape character decisions and drive the plot forward, making conflict a dominant structural element.

title: The Gate
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The subtitles reveal a sustained and escalating conflict with demonic forces unleashed by the characters' actions. The dialogue explicitly mentions 'demons,' 'sacrifices,' and the need to 'close the gate,' indicating a high-stakes battle against supernatural entities. The characters face constant threats, forcing them into strategic confrontations, as evidenced by lines like 'We have to close the gate' and 'We have to go to the hole and do it right.' The narrative revolves almost entirely around this central conflict, with character decisions driven by the need to survive and contain the demonic threat, culminating in a final confrontation where 'love and light' are used to combat the darkness.

title: The Bedroom Window
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The subtitles reveal a sustained antagonism between Terry and a suspected serial attacker, Chris Henderson, escalating from Terry's initial witness account to a deliberate attempt to bait and capture Henderson. This conflict drives Terry's actions, including his interactions with the police, his relationship with Sylvia, and his eventual decision to take matters into his own hands. The dialogue explicitly mentions threats, danger, and escalating tension, such as when Terry says, "If it is, he may recur," and when Denise warns, "Denise, it becomes serious." The high stakes are evident as Terry risks his freedom and safety to stop Henderson, culminating in a violent confrontation and the death of Sylvia, further solidifying conflict as the central structural element.

title: The Fourth Protocol
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The subtitles reveal a sustained antagonism between British intelligence and Soviet agents, with explicit threats of nuclear war. The narrative is driven by the escalating tension of preventing a bomb plot, as evidenced by dialogue such as "That's... that's a detonator for a bomb. A bomb? An atomic bomb." and "If an atomic bomb explodes on an American base... That will destroy NATO." The characters' decisions are shaped by the high-stakes opposition, with Preston's pursuit of Petrofsky and Karpov's internal power struggles within the KGB forming the core of the plot. The film is structured around sustained confrontation, strategic maneuvering, and the looming threat of catastrophic violence.

title: Less than Zero
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The subtitles reveal a persistent antagonism between Julian and Rip, driven by Julian's drug debt: "I just want my 50K." This conflict escalates as Rip pressures Julian: "You owe me a lot of cash. I'm carrying you like I'm stupid." Clay becomes entangled, attempting to protect Julian from Rip's threats: "You just leave him alone, asshole." The narrative culminates in a violent confrontation, highlighting the high stakes and sustained opposition: "Rip did this." The film's progression is almost entirely shaped by this central conflict and its consequences.

title: Back to the Beach
justification: Structural conflict is a central engine of the film's narrative. The film revolves around multiple conflicts: Bobby's identity crisis and his strained relationship with his parents, the parents' marital issues stemming from the father's obsession with the past and work, Sandi's unconventional lifestyle clashing with her parents' expectations, and the escalating rivalry between the father and Zed, culminating in a surfing competition. Dialogue such as "He keeps needling me," and "Stop it, boys!" highlights the ongoing tension within the family. The threat of the "Humunga Cowabunga" wave and the surfing competition create high stakes, driving character decisions and narrative progression. The film's resolution hinges on resolving these conflicts, solidifying their structural importance.

title: Fatal Beauty
justification: The film's narrative is overwhelmingly driven by conflict. The subtitles reveal a sustained battle against drug trafficking, featuring recurring threats, escalating violence, and strategic confrontations. Rizzoli's investigation of Kroll's drug operation leads to multiple shootouts, betrayals, and escalating stakes, as evidenced by dialogue such as "You're dead meat!" and "I'll kick your black ass back to Africa!" The conflict intensifies with the introduction of 'fatal beauty,' a deadly drug causing widespread deaths, further fueling Rizzoli's determination and placing her in constant danger. The narrative culminates in a final confrontation with Kroll, solidifying conflict as the dominant structural engine.

title: The Mosquito Coast
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The central conflict revolves around the protagonist's (Mr. Fox) sustained antagonism towards modern American society, which he views as decadent and corrupt. This antagonism drives his decision to uproot his family and establish a 'superior civilization' in the Mosquito Coast. The narrative is then propelled by escalating conflicts: with locals, missionaries ('State your business, Reverend'), and ultimately, the environment itself ('Rain gonna wash the experiment out to sea'). The film culminates in a violent confrontation and the destruction of Mr. Fox's utopian vision, highlighting the centrality of conflict to the plot's progression.

title: Extreme Prejudice
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of this film's narrative. The subtitles reveal persistent antagonism between Jack Benteen, a Texas Ranger, and Cash Bailey, a drug kingpin, escalating from border skirmishes to a final showdown. Explicit threats and danger are constant, as evidenced by lines like "You cross the river, your ass is mine" and the numerous gunfights. Sustained confrontation is evident in the strategic maneuvering between Benteen and Bailey, as well as the military operation to rob the bank. High-stakes opposition shapes character decisions, such as Benteen's pursuit of Bailey despite personal risks and Sarita's divided loyalties. The entire plot revolves around this central conflict, making it the primary driver of narrative progression.

title: Light of Day
justification: Structural conflict is a central engine in this film. The narrative revolves around Patti's struggles and her contentious relationships with her family, particularly her brother Joe and her mother. This is evident in dialogues where Joe confronts Patti about stealing tools and her general instability. The conflict escalates with Patti's mother's illness, leading to further tension and disagreements about her care and Patti's role in Benji's life. The film culminates in a confrontation about Patti's lifestyle and its impact on her family, highlighting the sustained antagonism that drives the narrative.

title: Cinderella
justification: The film's narrative is significantly driven by conflict, primarily revolving around themes of appearance, jealousy, and the consequences of plastic surgery. The dialogue reveals escalating tension and antagonism between characters, such as the initial argument between Hyunsu and her mother, and later conflicts among Hyunsu and her friends, particularly Sungeun. Sukyung's distress over her changed face and subsequent self-harm introduce a darker, more intense conflict. The recurring motif of wanting to be 'pretty' fuels much of the interpersonal conflict and shapes character decisions, making conflict a central, though not exclusive, engine of the story.

title: Someone to Watch Over Me
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The central conflict revolves around Claire Gregory, a material witness, and Joey Venza, the man she must identify. Venza's threats, escape from custody, and relentless pursuit of Claire create sustained tension and danger, as evidenced by dialogue such as "Venza's either going to skip or get to her." The escalating conflict forces Detective Keegan to protect Claire, leading to a direct confrontation with Venza in the climax: "Venza wants you. You for Ellie and Tommy." The narrative is almost entirely driven by this antagonism, shaping character decisions and plot progression, making conflict the primary structural element.

title: No Mercy
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The subtitles reveal a sustained antagonism between Eddie, a Chicago cop, and various criminal elements, particularly a New Orleans gangster named Losado. The narrative escalates from a small-time drug bust to a murder investigation, with Eddie pursuing Losado and his associates. Dialogue such as "I'm looking for the bastard that gutted my partner and tied his intestines around his neck. And with or without your help, I'm gonna get him" and Losado's threats like "You'll die, my friend!" demonstrate the high stakes and sustained confrontation driving the plot. The conflict shapes Eddie's decisions and actions throughout the film, making it the central element of the story.

title: Disorderlies
justification: The film's narrative is overwhelmingly driven by conflict. The central conflict revolves around Lowry's debt to Luis Montana and his attempts to inherit his uncle's fortune to repay it. This leads to a series of escalating conflicts, including hiring inept orderlies to hasten his uncle's death, dealing with the consequences of their actions, and ultimately facing threats from both Montana and his own nephew, Winslow. The subtitles are filled with explicit threats ('People die from that disease, Lowry'), strategic confrontations (Lowry's attempts to manipulate events), and high-stakes opposition, making conflict the dominant engine of the story.

title: Maid to Order
justification: Structural conflict is a central engine of the film's narrative. The core conflict arises from Jessie's irresponsible behavior and her father's disappointment, leading to a fairy godmother's intervention that strips Jessie of her identity and wealth. This sets up a sustained antagonistic situation where Jessie must overcome her spoiled nature to regain her former life, as evidenced by Stella's statement: "It is unless you clean up your act." Jessie faces constant challenges, such as being rejected by her father and friends, and struggling to adapt to a life of poverty and hard work, as shown in her dialogue: "Daddy, I'm so glad to see you!" and "Daddy, I said I was sorry, dammit." The narrative progresses through Jessie's attempts to change and prove herself, making conflict the primary driver.

title: The Hidden
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The subtitles depict a relentless pursuit of alien entities inhabiting human bodies, driving nearly all plot progression. The dialogue is saturated with escalating tension, explicit threats, and sustained confrontation, as evidenced by phrases like "Freeze!", "High speed pursuit", "armed and dangerous", and repeated instances of violence. The central conflict shapes character decisions, particularly those of Beck and Gallagher, who are constantly strategizing and engaging in high-stakes opposition. The narrative revolves around stopping the alien threat, making conflict the primary driver of the story.

title: From the Hip
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of this film's narrative. The subtitles reveal a sustained antagonism between Robin, a young lawyer, and the established legal system, exemplified by his firm and opposing counsel. This is evident in Robin's unethical actions to secure a case, his contentious courtroom tactics, and his ultimate decision to expose his client's guilt, defying legal norms. The Benoit case itself presents a high-stakes conflict, with the potential for a death penalty. The escalating tension between Robin and Benoit, culminating in Benoit's confession, drives the narrative to its climax. Robin's internal conflict between his ambition and his moral compass further fuels the story's progression.

title: The Last Emperor
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The subtitles reveal persistent antagonism between Pu Yi and various opposing forces, including the Republican government, the Japanese, and ultimately, the Communist regime. Explicit threats and escalating tension are evident throughout, from his initial imprisonment and forced abdication to his manipulation by the Japanese and subsequent re-education as a war criminal. Sustained confrontation shapes Pu Yi's decisions, as he navigates political turmoil and personal struggles, with the high-stakes opposition driving nearly all narrative progression. The dialogue highlights his powerlessness and constant struggle for control, making conflict the central element.

title: Teen Wolf Too
justification: Structural conflict is a dominant force in this narrative. The central plot revolves around Todd's struggle to navigate a sports scholarship he doesn't deserve, leading to sustained antagonism with Coach Finstock, who threatens his position. Todd faces escalating tension as he tries to balance academic expectations with the demands of boxing, further complicated by his werewolf transformation. The boxing matches themselves are explicit physical confrontations that drive the plot forward, culminating in a high-stakes championship bout. Dean Dunn's manipulation and threats add another layer of institutional conflict, making opposition a central engine of the story.

title: Who Framed Roger Rabbit?
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The subtitles reveal a sustained antagonism between Judge Doom and the toons, escalating into an explicit threat of annihilation via "The Dip," as Doom seeks to destroy Toontown. This conflict drives the plot, shaping Eddie Valiant's decisions as he investigates Acme's murder and attempts to protect Roger Rabbit from Doom's relentless pursuit. The narrative is structured around this central conflict, with recurring confrontations, strategic maneuvering, and high stakes that directly influence character actions and the overall progression of the story, such as the weasels' constant attempts to capture Roger and Doom's plan to dismantle the Red Car.

title: Coming to America
justification: Structural conflict is a central theme in this film. The primary conflict arises from Prince Akeem's desire to choose his own wife versus the traditions and expectations of his royal family and kingdom. This is evident in dialogues where Akeem expresses his dissatisfaction with arranged marriages and the rose petals. The conflict escalates when Akeem travels to America to find a wife who loves him for himself, leading to clashes with his father, who disapproves of his choices and the woman he falls in love with. The tension culminates in a confrontation between Akeem and his father, who arrives in America to enforce the arranged marriage, creating a high-stakes situation that drives the narrative forward.

title: Good Morning Vietnam
justification: Structural conflict is a central engine driving the narrative. The subtitles reveal persistent antagonism between Cronauer and Sergeant Major Dickerson, who threatens Cronauer explicitly: "if you toy with me, I'll burn you so bad you'll wish you died as a child." This conflict escalates as Dickerson disapproves of Cronauer's humor and broadcasting style. Furthermore, the film presents the overarching conflict of the Vietnam War, with dialogue referencing the Viet Cong, bombings, and unsafe routes, creating a backdrop of danger and tension that shapes character decisions and narrative progression. The bombing at Jimmy Wah's and the revelation of Tuan's involvement as a VC terrorist further intensify the conflict, directly impacting Cronauer's relationships and forcing him to confront the complexities of the war.

title: Big
justification: Structural conflict is a dominant force in "Big." The narrative is propelled by Josh's struggle to revert to his child self after wishing to be 'big.' This is evident in his interactions with his mother, who doesn't recognize him ("WHERE IS MY CHILD?"), and his best friend, Billy, who initially disbelieves him ("HELP! HELP!"). Josh faces constant challenges navigating the adult world, including securing a job and managing relationships, all while trying to find the Zoltar machine to undo the wish. The escalating tension between his desire to return home and the complications of his adult life, including his relationship with Susan and professional rivalry with Paul, drive the plot forward, making conflict central to the narrative's progression.

title: Crocodile Dundee 2
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The central conflict revolves around Sue Charlton being targeted by Luis Rico, a drug lord, because her ex-husband possesses incriminating evidence against him. This conflict escalates rapidly, with explicit threats made against Sue's life ('Get rid of him, or your lady is a dead woman.'). Mick Dundee becomes embroiled in this conflict, actively working to protect Sue and retrieve the evidence ('You just hang on.'). The narrative progresses through sustained antagonism, strategic confrontations, and escalating danger, culminating in a final showdown at Mick's property in the Northern Territory.

title: Cocktail
justification: Structural conflict is a central theme, primarily manifested through Brian's struggle to achieve financial success and navigate complex relationships. He faces repeated rejections in his job search ("Your résumé's completely inadequate.") and academic setbacks ("Bankrupt!"). A significant conflict arises with his mentor, Doug, fueled by competition and differing views on success and relationships, culminating in a physical altercation ("You fuckin' son of a bitch!"). Brian also experiences conflict with Jordan's wealthy father, who disapproves of their relationship and attempts to buy him off ("I don't want your goddamn money."). These conflicts drive Brian's decisions and shape the narrative's progression.

title: Moonstruck
justification: Structural conflict is a central engine driving the narrative. The film revolves around Loretta's engagement to Johnny and the subsequent complications arising from his family dynamics, particularly his estranged brother Ronny. The dialogue reveals a history of 'bad blood' between the brothers, stemming from an accident where Johnny inadvertently caused Ronny to lose his hand and his fiancée. This conflict escalates as Loretta becomes entangled with Ronny, leading to an affair and threatening her engagement. The tension is further heightened by Cosmo's marital issues and his questioning of love and fidelity, adding another layer of conflict that shapes character decisions and narrative progression. The resolution involves Loretta choosing Ronny, highlighting how conflict dictates the romantic trajectory.

title: Die Hard
justification: The film's narrative is overwhelmingly driven by sustained conflict. From the moment John McClane arrives, the Nakatomi Plaza is seized by terrorists, immediately establishing a high-stakes antagonistic situation. The dialogue is saturated with threats, strategic maneuvering, and escalating violence, as evidenced by lines like, "Ladies and gentlemen... they're about to be taught a lesson in the real use of power" and "I now have a machine gun. Ho... ho... ho." McClane's repeated confrontations with the terrorists, his attempts to thwart their plans, and the constant threat to the hostages form the central engine of the story. The conflict is not merely background noise; it dictates nearly every major plot development and character decision, making it the dominant structural element.

title: Beetle Juice
justification: Structural conflict is a central engine of the film. The narrative is driven by the antagonism between the Maitlands (ghosts) and the Deetzes (living family) who move into their house, creating escalating tension as both sides attempt to displace the other. The Maitlands' initial attempts to scare the Deetzes away fail, leading them to seek help from Betelgeuse, a 'bio-exorcist,' which introduces a new layer of conflict and threat. The Deetzes, in turn, exploit the supernatural events for personal gain, further intensifying the conflict. The high stakes are evident as the Maitlands risk 'death for the dead' (exorcism) and Lydia Deetz contemplates joining the afterlife to escape her family, highlighting how conflict shapes character decisions and drives the narrative forward.

title: Twins
justification: Structural conflict is a central element in "Twins." The narrative is driven by Julius's search for his brother Vincent, who is entangled with loan sharks and a stolen fuel-injection system. Dialogue reveals Vincent owes $20,000 to the Klane brothers, creating immediate threat and urgency. This debt forces Vincent into criminal activity, escalating the stakes. The Klane brothers' pursuit of Vincent and Julius's attempts to protect him result in physical confrontations, such as the fight at the bar and the final showdown with Beetroot McKinley, highlighting sustained antagonism. The film's climax involves a dangerous exchange and a violent confrontation, solidifying conflict as a primary driver of the plot.

title: Oliver & Company
justification: Structural conflict is highly salient in this film, driving nearly all narrative progression. The central conflict revolves around Fagin's debt to Sykes, creating a constant threat and high stakes. This is evident in dialogues like "The money, Fagin" and "People like you get hurt." The kidnapping plot escalates the conflict, as seen in the ransom note and Sykes's threats. The climax involves a chase and confrontation, solidifying conflict as the dominant engine of the story, with the protagonists actively opposing Sykes and his dogs to rescue Jenny.

title: A Fish Called Wanda
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The subtitles reveal a sustained antagonism between the core group of criminals, driven by greed and mistrust, as they attempt to steal and then secure a large sum of money. This is evident in lines like "Anybody moves and you're dead" and the constant betrayals and double-crosses, such as Wanda's affair with Archie to discover the location of the diamonds. The escalating tension is clear as the characters attempt to outwit each other and the police, with lines like "Police! Open up!" and the constant threat of exposure or violence. The high stakes are emphasized by the value of the diamonds and the consequences of getting caught, shaping character decisions and driving the plot forward, as seen in the numerous attempts to kill or betray each other.

title: Willow
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The subtitles reveal a persistent antagonism between Queen Bavmorda and the prophecy surrounding Elora Danan, driving the plot forward. Bavmorda's explicit threats to kill Elora and maintain her reign of terror create escalating tension. Sustained confrontation is evident in the recurring battles between Bavmorda's forces and those protecting Elora, shaping character decisions and narrative progression. The high stakes of Elora's survival and Bavmorda's downfall are constantly emphasized, making conflict the central element.

title: The Naked Gun: From the Files of Police Squad!
justification: The film's narrative is overwhelmingly driven by conflict. The central plot revolves around preventing an assassination attempt on Queen Elizabeth, orchestrated by Vincent Ludwig. This threat escalates throughout the film, with multiple attempts on Nordberg's life and Frank Drebin's investigation constantly facing opposition. The conflict is sustained through physical confrontations, strategic maneuvering, and psychological tension, shaping character decisions and driving the plot forward. The dialogue explicitly reveals the assassination plot ("20,000,000 deposited... upon proof of Queen's death") and the escalating danger, making conflict the dominant structural engine.

title: Scrooged
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative.
