The narrative revolves around the escalating conflict, with President Coin and Plutarch strategizing to use Katniss as the Mockingjay to unite the districts against President Snow, who in turn uses Peeta as a weapon against Katniss. The film is structured around this sustained opposition and the high stakes involved, with the characters' decisions driven by the overarching conflict.

title: Captain America: The Winter Soldier
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the narrative. The film is driven by persistent antagonism between Captain America and HYDRA, which has infiltrated S.H.I.E.L.D. This is evident from dialogues such as Steve Rogers' warning: "S.H.I.E.L.D. is not what we thought it was. It's been taken over by HYDRA. Alexander Pierce is their leader." The film escalates tension through explicit threats, danger, and sustained confrontation, as seen in the numerous fight sequences and strategic confrontations. The high-stakes opposition shapes character decisions, particularly Steve's decision to dismantle S.H.I.E.L.D. to eliminate HYDRA's influence, as well as his conflict with the Winter Soldier.

title: The Lego Movie
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The primary conflict involves the Master Builders, led by Emmet, against Lord Business, who seeks to freeze the universe with the Kragle. This antagonism is established early with Vitruvius's confrontation with Lord Business and the prophecy of the 'Special One' who can thwart the Kragle. The film is then driven by the escalating tension as Lord Business hunts down the Master Builders and attempts to deploy the Kragle, while Emmet and his allies actively resist and strategize to stop him. The stakes are extremely high, with the fate of the entire universe hanging in the balance, making conflict the central driving force.

title: Transformers: Age of Extinction
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of this film's narrative. The subtitles reveal a persistent antagonism between humans and Transformers, escalating into a global hunt for Autobots led by the CIA's 'Cemetery Wind' unit ('All Autobots are being hunted. We're all in danger.'). This conflict drives character decisions, as Cade Yeager chooses to protect Optimus Prime, leading to sustained confrontation with government forces ('Mr. Yeager, my name's James Savoy. I'm a federal agent. My men and I are trying to track down an abandoned truck.'). The emergence of Galvatron and his Decepticons further intensifies the conflict, threatening global destruction and forcing Autobots and humans into a high-stakes alliance ('Detonate the Seed in the largest city.').

title: Maleficent
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The initial conflict between the human kingdom and the Moors establishes a sustained antagonism. Stefan's betrayal of Maleficent and his subsequent rise to power through violence creates a central conflict that drives Maleficent's actions. The curse placed on Aurora escalates the tension and shapes the narrative for sixteen years, with the threat of its fulfillment constantly looming. The film culminates in a direct confrontation between Maleficent and King Stefan, solidifying conflict as the primary structural element.

title: X-Men: Days of Future Past
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The subtitles depict a future ravaged by war between mutants and Sentinels, establishing a high-stakes conflict from the outset. The core plot revolves around preventing this dystopian future by altering past events, specifically Mystique's actions in 1973. This creates a sustained antagonistic dynamic, with the protagonists racing against time to avert a catastrophic outcome. Dialogue such as "Fighting an enemy we cannot defeat" and "We have no escape. This is our last chance" underscores the severity and centrality of the conflict, driving character decisions and narrative progression.

title: Dawn of the Planet of the Apes
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The subtitles depict a world ravaged by a virus, leading to a power struggle between humans and evolved apes. The initial conflict arises from the apes' escape and the subsequent fear and aggression from humans, exemplified by Carver shooting an ape. This escalates into a full-blown confrontation, with both sides preparing for war, as Dreyfus states, "Well, then we fight them." The narrative revolves around attempts to prevent this war, but ultimately, betrayal and escalating violence make conflict unavoidable, culminating in a large-scale battle and the separation of the two groups.

title: Big Hero 6
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The central conflict arises from the theft of Hiro's microbots, which escalates into a revenge plot by Professor Callaghan, who uses the stolen technology to seek retribution for his daughter's death. This antagonism drives the plot forward, forcing Hiro and his friends to confront Callaghan in a series of escalating confrontations. The stakes are consistently high, involving potential destruction and loss of life, as evidenced by dialogue such as "You're going to watch everything you've built disappear. Then, it's your turn." The narrative revolves around the heroes' attempts to stop Callaghan, making conflict the primary driver of character decisions and plot progression.

title: The Amazing Spider-Man 2
justification: Structural conflict is a dominant force in this narrative. The film is driven by persistent antagonism between Spider-Man and various villains, including Electro and the Green Goblin, with escalating threats and sustained confrontations. The subtitles highlight explicit dangers, such as the plutonium hijacking and Electro's threat to plunge the city into darkness. High-stakes opposition shapes Peter Parker's decisions, forcing him to balance his personal life with his responsibilities as Spider-Man. The narrative progression is heavily reliant on these conflicts, making structural conflict a central engine of the story.

title: Godzilla
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The subtitles reveal a persistent antagonism between humanity and the MUTOs, escalating from initial encounters to large-scale battles. The threat of nuclear destruction and the MUTOs' reproductive imperative create high stakes, driving character decisions and plot progression. Sustained confrontation is evident in military operations, strategic planning, and physical combat, with the conflict shaping nearly all major developments, including the search for the MUTOs, attempts to disarm the warhead, and the final showdown in San Francisco. The dialogue emphasizes the escalating danger and the need to restore balance, solidifying conflict as the central structural element.

title: 22 Jump Street
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The central plot revolves around Schmidt and Jenko's persistent antagonism with drug dealers, escalating from campus-level distribution to confronting the Ghost, a major trafficker. Explicit threats and danger are constant, as seen in the numerous shootouts and chases: "I'm going to shoot them in the face for that! That was our fucking car!" The film sustains confrontation through undercover operations, strategic planning, and physical altercations, all driven by the high-stakes opposition to criminal activity. The narrative progression is almost entirely shaped by this sustained antagonism and the escalating threats, making conflict the primary driver.

title: Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The central conflict revolves around the antagonism between the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles and the Foot Clan, led by Shredder. This conflict escalates throughout the film, with explicit threats and escalating tension, such as Shredder's plan to unleash toxins on New York City. Sustained confrontations, both physical and strategic, drive the plot, as seen in the subway fight, the attack on the turtles' lair, and the final showdown at Sacks Tower. The high stakes of saving the city shape the characters' decisions and actions, making conflict the primary driver of narrative progression.

title: The Hobbit: The Battle of the Five Armies
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The subtitles are saturated with antagonism, threats, and sustained confrontations. The initial conflict is the dragon Smaug's attack, leading to the destruction of Lake-town and the dwarves' quest to reclaim Erebor. This immediately escalates into a multi-sided conflict involving dwarves, men, elves, and ultimately, orcs. Dialogue such as "They've woken the dragon!" and "The battle for the Mountain is about to begin" explicitly highlights the centrality of conflict. The film culminates in a massive battle, with characters constantly facing danger and making high-stakes decisions, as evidenced by lines like "Fight to the death!" and "We're going to take out their leader."

title: Interstellar
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The subtitles reveal a sustained, escalating conflict against environmental collapse, driving the characters' decisions and actions. The initial conflict is humanity's struggle against the blight and dust storms, explicitly stated as a threat to survival: "The last people to starve will be the first to suffocate." This conflict escalates as NASA secretly plans to abandon Earth, leading to moral and strategic conflicts about the mission's true purpose. The conflict reaches a climax with Dr. Mann's betrayal and the desperate fight for survival near Gargantua, where characters face life-or-death choices under extreme pressure.

title: How to Train Your Dragon 2
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The primary conflict revolves around Drago Bludvist's ambition to build a dragon army and conquer the world, which directly threatens Berk and its newfound peace with dragons. This threat escalates throughout the film, driving character decisions and plot developments, as seen in Stoick's initial decision to fortify Berk and Hiccup's determination to confront Drago. The conflict is sustained through physical confrontations, strategic planning, and psychological tension, such as the capture of dragons and riders, the battle at the dragon sanctuary, and the climactic showdown where Drago controls Toothless. The death of Stoick further intensifies the conflict, solidifying it as the central driving force of the narrative.

title: Gone Girl
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The subtitles reveal a sustained and escalating antagonism between Nick and Amy, beginning with subtle marital tensions and culminating in explicit threats and violence. Amy's disappearance and the subsequent investigation create a high-stakes opposition, with Nick as the primary suspect. The dialogue showcases Amy's elaborate plan to frame Nick for her murder, highlighting a strategic confrontation that drives the plot forward. The film concludes with a chilling resolution where conflict persists, shaping the characters' decisions and ensuring a future defined by sustained antagonism.

title: Divergent
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The subtitles reveal a society rigidly divided into factions, with underlying tensions and power struggles, particularly between Abnegation and Erudite, as evidenced by the dialogue about Erudite's ambition to govern and accusations against Abnegation. The aptitude tests and Choosing Ceremony create immediate high stakes, forcing characters to make life-altering decisions under pressure. The Dauntless initiation process is inherently adversarial, with constant competition, physical challenges, and the threat of being cut and becoming Factionless. This culminates in a full-scale armed conflict initiated by Erudite against Abnegation, with Dauntless soldiers under mind control, driving the protagonists to fight for survival and to dismantle the system of control.

title: Neighbors
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The central conflict revolves around Mac and Kelly's escalating antagonism with the fraternity Delta Psi, next door. This conflict begins with noise complaints and escalates to elaborate pranks, sabotage, and even dangerous situations involving their baby. The narrative is almost entirely driven by the back-and-forth between the couple and the fraternity, with each side attempting to outdo the other. Dialogue such as "We need to go over there. We need to fucking tell them not to do that. Right now." and "We're gonna fucking fuck them!" demonstrates the sustained antagonism that shapes the plot.

title: Ride Along
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The subtitles are saturated with antagonism, threats, and sustained confrontations. The film revolves around a central conflict: the pursuit and takedown of the elusive criminal, Omar, by law enforcement. This pursuit involves numerous escalating conflicts, including shootouts with Serbian arms dealers ('Everybody down! Atlanta PD!'), confrontations with gang members ('You think you're tough because you're in a little gang?'), and internal conflicts within the police department ('I'm shortening your leash, James.'). The high stakes of capturing Omar and the constant threat of violence drive character decisions and propel the narrative forward, making conflict the primary structural element.

title: Rio 2
justification: Structural conflict is a central engine driving the narrative. The primary conflict arises from the threat of illegal logging endangering the macaw's habitat, which escalates as the loggers actively seek to eliminate the birds. This is compounded by an internal conflict between Blu's domesticated lifestyle and Jewel's desire for a wild existence, leading to disagreements and high-stakes decisions about their family's future. Nigel, the vengeful cockatoo, serves as a persistent antagonist, actively plotting against Blu and his family, creating escalating tension and direct confrontation. The film culminates in a large-scale battle between the macaws and the loggers, with Nigel adding to the chaos, making conflict the dominant force shaping the narrative's progression.

title: Lucy
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The subtitles reveal a sustained and escalating conflict between Lucy and Mr. Jang's organization after she is unwillingly turned into a drug mule ('Take this off me right now! I can't, Mr. Jang's the only one who has the key.'). This initial conflict escalates into physical violence, pursuit, and strategic maneuvering as Lucy seeks to control her condition and transmit her knowledge ('There are men coming here. Can you secure the room? I need to stay focused.'). The narrative is almost entirely driven by the threat posed by Mr. Jang and Lucy's efforts to evade and counteract him, making conflict the central organizing principle.

title: Lone Survivor
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The subtitles depict a sustained military operation against a high-value Taliban target, Ahmad Shah, immediately establishing an antagonistic force. The narrative escalates rapidly from reconnaissance to a fierce firefight, with explicit threats and escalating tension evident in lines like "Request immediate QRF! Troops in contact!" and "We need immediate air support." The high stakes are underscored by the constant struggle for survival, the loss of communication, and the desperate attempts to call for extraction. The film culminates in a devastating battle and rescue, making conflict the central driving force.

title: The Fault in Our Stars
justification: Structural conflict is a central engine of the film, primarily manifested through the characters' battles with terminal illnesses and the emotional and existential challenges they face. The dialogue frequently revolves around the characters' struggles with cancer, treatment side effects, and the fear of oblivion, creating persistent tension and shaping their decisions. Hazel's internal conflict about her illness and its impact on her family is evident in lines like, "Depression's not a side effect of cancer. It's a side effect of dying." Augustus's fear of oblivion and desire to leave a mark are recurring themes, as seen in his statement, "I intend to live an extraordinary life. To be remembered." The conflict with Peter Van Houten, though brief, is a significant plot point, highlighting the characters' need for closure and meaning in the face of death. The escalating health crises, such as Hazel's lung issues and Augustus's cancer recurrence, further intensify the structural conflict.

title: Mr. Peabody & Sherman
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The central conflict revolves around Mr. Peabody's fitness as a parent, challenged by Ms. Grunion, who seeks to permanently remove Sherman from his custody. This threat escalates throughout the film, driving Peabody's actions and decisions. Further conflicts arise from their time-traveling adventures, such as Penny's near-marriage to King Tut and Sherman's involvement in the Trojan War, each presenting immediate dangers and high stakes. The climax involves a rip in the space-time continuum, requiring Peabody and Sherman to work together to save the world, solidifying conflict as the primary driver of the plot.

title: 300: Rise of an Empire
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The subtitles are saturated with antagonism between the Greeks and Persians, escalating threats of invasion and destruction ("Sparta will fall. All of Greece will fall. And Persian fire will reduce Athens to cinder."), and sustained confrontation in naval battles. The high stakes of national survival shape character decisions, particularly Themistokles's strategic choices and Artemisia's ruthless ambition. The entire plot revolves around the impending war and the strategic maneuvering of both sides, making conflict the central driving force.

title: The Maze Runner
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The entire plot revolves around the Gladers' struggle against the mysterious forces that trapped them in the Maze. This antagonism is evident from the beginning, with characters constantly facing threats from the Maze itself, the Grievers, and the changing environment. The high stakes are emphasized by the constant danger and the fact that no one has ever survived a night in the Maze. The film escalates as the Gladers confront these dangers, attempt to escape, and ultimately face the organization behind their imprisonment, making conflict the central driving force.

title: Noah
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The subtitles reveal a sustained antagonism between Noah and the descendants of Cain, who seek to exploit the earth's resources and dominate others. This conflict escalates with Tubal-cain's repeated threats and attempts to seize the ark, culminating in a violent confrontation during the flood. Internal conflict is also present, as Noah grapples with his understanding of the Creator's will and his perceived duty to end humanity, leading to intense opposition from his family. The high stakes of survival against both human and environmental forces drive nearly all major plot developments and character decisions, making conflict the central organizing principle.

title: The Equalizer
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The subtitles reveal a sustained and escalating conflict between the protagonist, Robert McCall, and a criminal organization led by Pushkin. This conflict begins with McCall's intervention to protect Alina from abuse, leading to a series of retaliatory actions and escalating violence. Dialogue such as "You took out the East Coast hub of Vladimir Pushkin," and threats like "My men there will kill them in 30 minutes" demonstrate the high stakes and persistent antagonism. The narrative progresses almost entirely through confrontations, strategic maneuvers, and the escalating threat to McCall and those he seeks to protect, making conflict the central driving force.

title: Edge of Tomorrow
justification: The film's narrative is overwhelmingly driven by conflict. The dialogue establishes an ongoing war against alien invaders ('mimics') who pose an existential threat to humanity. The subtitles are filled with descriptions of battles, casualties, and strategic planning to defeat the enemy. The central character, Cage, is forced into combat and repeatedly relives the same day, constantly fighting and dying in an effort to change the outcome of the war. The escalating tension and high stakes are evident in lines like 'All of humanity's at stake' and the constant references to the impending invasion and potential defeat.

title: Non-Stop
justification: The film's narrative is almost entirely driven by escalating conflict. The central premise revolves around a series of threatening texts demanding money, coupled with the threat of passenger deaths. This creates persistent antagonism as the protagonist, Bill Marks, races against time to identify and neutralize the threat. The conflict escalates with each passing deadline, leading to physical confrontations, suspicion, and ultimately, the discovery of a bomb. The high stakes of saving the plane and its passengers make conflict the dominant engine of the story, shaping character decisions and driving the plot forward.

title: Heaven is for Real
justification: Structural conflict is a central engine in this film, primarily revolving around the Burpo family's financial struggles, Todd's health issues, and the controversy surrounding Colton's claims of visiting heaven. The family faces escalating financial difficulties, as evidenced by dialogue such as "How tight are we this month?" and "$23,000." Todd's health problems, including a broken leg and kidney stones, create recurring crises and impact his ability to provide for his family and lead his church. The conflict surrounding Colton's experiences is sustained through skepticism from the community and church leadership, as seen in the church board's concerns and the newspaper article. The film's narrative progression is significantly shaped by these conflicts, driving character decisions and creating tension.

title: Fury
justification: The film's narrative is overwhelmingly driven by sustained conflict. From the opening scene of taking fire in the woods to the final stand at the crossroads, the subtitles depict constant antagonism between American soldiers and German forces. Explicit threats and escalating tension are pervasive, as evidenced by lines like "They're waiting for the tanks" and "That's a goddamn Tiger!" Sustained confrontation is central, including physical battles ("Enemy fire from our right flank") and psychological struggles (the constant pressure on Norman to kill). The high stakes of war shape every character decision, and the conflict serves as the primary engine of the story, with nearly all narrative progression driven by sustained antagonism or threat.

title: Dumb and Dumber To
justification: Structural conflict is a central engine driving the narrative. The film revolves around Harry's need for a kidney transplant, which creates a high-stakes objective. This need fuels a road trip and escalating confrontations, including encounters with criminals, deceitful characters, and ultimately, a violent showdown. Dialogue such as "I need a kidney transplant" and "If I can't find another kidney real soon, I'm dead meat" underscores the urgency and stakes. The pursuit of Penny and the box further intensifies the conflict, with characters actively opposing each other to achieve their goals, as seen in the dialogue "I want them dead, now!" and the final confrontation with Adele and Lippincott.

title: Tammy
justification: Structural conflict is a dominant engine in this film. The narrative is initiated by Tammy's abrupt firing, which immediately escalates into a heated confrontation with her boss, Keith. This initial conflict triggers a chain of further conflicts: Tammy discovers her husband's infidelity, leading to a volatile confrontation with him and her neighbor, Missi. The central plot revolves around Tammy and her grandmother's escape, which is fraught with constant arguments, petty theft, and encounters with antagonistic characters. The film sustains a high level of tension through Tammy's repeated clashes with authority figures, her grandmother's erratic behavior, and the looming threat of legal consequences for their actions.

title: Annabelle
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The subtitles reveal a sustained and escalating conflict with a demonic entity. This conflict begins with subtle disturbances ('It started out small...like a hand or a leg was in a different position') and quickly escalates to explicit threats and violence ('Get out of here, Mia!'). The central characters are in constant opposition to this force, making decisions driven by the need to protect themselves and their child ('We have to get rid of it'). The narrative culminates in a high-stakes confrontation where a soul is demanded, solidifying conflict as the primary driver of the plot.

title: Let’s Be Cops
justification: The film's narrative is heavily driven by conflict, primarily between the protagonists and a criminal organization. This conflict escalates throughout the film, starting with a hit-and-run incident ("You hit my car.") and culminating in a dangerous confrontation with a mob boss and corrupt police officers ("Mossi has got Ryan, and he is gonna kill him."). The protagonists' decisions are largely shaped by this escalating conflict, as they attempt to navigate their fake police personas while facing real threats. The dialogue reveals sustained antagonism and escalating tension, making conflict the dominant structural engine of the film.

title: The Monuments Men
justification: Structural conflict is a central engine driving the narrative. The film revolves around the Monuments Men's mission to protect and recover art stolen by the Nazis during World War II, which inherently involves persistent antagonism. The team faces explicit threats and danger in a war zone, as evidenced by dialogue such as warnings about real bullets during training and the constant risk of enemy encounters ('Walk carefully, take no undue chances'). Sustained confrontation is present, not only in physical skirmishes (like the encounter with German soldiers) but also in strategic opposition to the Nazi regime's art theft ('That's what Hitler wants. And it's the one thing we simply can't allow.'). The Nero Decree introduces an escalating threat of total destruction, further emphasizing the high stakes. The conflict shapes character decisions, as seen in their determination to recover art despite the risks and losses.

title: Penguins of Madagascar
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The central conflict revolves around the penguins' repeated confrontations with Dave, an octopus seeking revenge for being overshadowed by them. This antagonism drives the plot forward, as Dave actively kidnaps and transforms penguins, creating escalating tension and danger. The penguins' decisions and actions are consistently shaped by their opposition to Dave, making conflict the primary driver of narrative progression. Dialogue such as "The only thing that has kept me going all these years... is my burning thirst for revenge!" and Dave's repeated attempts to capture and transform the penguins highlight the sustained antagonism.

title: The Purge: Anarchy
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The Purge itself establishes a premise of sanctioned violence and antagonism, creating immediate high stakes. The protagonists face escalating threats from multiple sources: initial car trouble leading to pursuit by violent Purgers, targeted attacks by a coordinated paramilitary group, and eventual capture and participation in a 'Purge auction.' The dialogue is saturated with explicit threats ('I'm gonna release the beast'), strategic planning for survival ('We need to run'), and desperate confrontations ('Diego, don't come back here. We have guns and we will shoot you.'). The characters' decisions are consistently shaped by the need to survive the night's violence, making conflict the central driver of plot progression.

title: Night at the Museum: Secret of the Tomb
justification: Structural conflict is a central engine in this narrative. The film is driven by the escalating threat to the tablet's magic and the characters' efforts to prevent its loss. This is evident in the dialogue: "We're in danger. There is a storm coming," and "If anyone disturbs this tomb...the end will come." The characters face sustained opposition from Sir Lancelot, who seeks to possess the tablet, leading to physical confrontations and strategic maneuvering. The high stakes are clear: "If the tablet dies...nothing can bring it back!" The narrative revolves around the characters' struggle to save the tablet and themselves, making conflict a dominant structural element.

title: Alexander and the Terrible, Horrible, No Good, Very Bad Day
justification: Structural conflict is a central engine in "Alexander and the Terrible, Horrible, No Good, Very Bad Day." The narrative revolves around a series of escalating misfortunes and challenges faced by the Cooper family. Alexander's initial wish for his family to experience a bad day sets off a chain of events, creating persistent antagonism between their desires and reality. This is evident in dialogues such as "This day is so cursed" and "What is wrong with you people?" which highlight the escalating tension and frustration. The family members face explicit threats to their personal goals, such as Emily's fear of missing her play and Anthony's prom plans being jeopardized, as shown in "Peter Pan can't have a cold, Dad" and "I'm not missing prom with Celia. I can't." The sustained confrontation with these obstacles shapes their decisions and drives the narrative forward, making conflict a dominant structural element.

title: Think Like a Man Too
justification: Structural conflict is a central engine of the film's narrative. The subtitles reveal persistent antagonism between the bachelor and bachelorette parties, escalating into strategic confrontations and sabotage (e.g., stealing the party bus, sabotaging the wedding plans). The high stakes of the wedding and the characters' desires create opposition that shapes decisions, such as Cedric's disastrous gambling spree to fund the bachelor party and the women's attempts to control the wedding arrangements. The conflict culminates in a bar fight and arrests, demonstrating how antagonism drives the plot. The dialogue highlights the escalating tension and recurring threats to the wedding, solidifying conflict's structural importance.

title: The Nut Job
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The central conflict revolves around the park's dire need for food and Surly's initial self-serving pursuit of the nut cart, which escalates into a sustained confrontation with both the park animals (led by Andie and Raccoon) and human criminals. The dialogue is filled with explicit threats, strategic maneuvering, and high-stakes opposition, such as Raccoon's plans to control the park's food supply and the human gang's bank heist. The escalating tension is evident in lines like, "We're at starvation levels! We're all gonna die!" and "These nuts are ours!" The narrative is almost entirely driven by the characters' attempts to secure food and overcome obstacles, making conflict the primary structural element.

title: Into the Woods
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The central plot revolves around the Baker and his wife's quest to break a witch's curse, requiring them to obtain specific items. This quest immediately introduces antagonism and escalating tension, as they must confront other characters and navigate dangerous situations. The conflict escalates further with the arrival of a giant, posing an explicit threat to the entire kingdom and forcing the characters into sustained confrontation. The characters' decisions are consistently shaped by the high-stakes opposition, making conflict the primary driver of narrative progression.

title: Unbroken
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The subtitles depict sustained antagonism and escalating tension throughout multiple phases of Zamperini's ordeal. Initially, there's the aerial combat with enemy fighters ('Zero, inbound, 10 o'clock, level'), followed by the struggle for survival at sea ('They don't know where we are. They'll find us. They'll never see us.'). The most prominent conflict arises in the POW camps, characterized by brutal treatment and psychological warfare from Watanabe ('You are enemies of Japan. You will be treated accordingly.'). Zamperini's defiance and Watanabe's escalating cruelty drive the narrative forward, making conflict the central element.

title: God’s Not Dead
justification: The film's narrative is heavily structured around conflict, primarily the central debate between Josh and Professor Radisson regarding the existence of God. This conflict escalates throughout the film, shaping Josh's decisions and relationships, most notably with his girlfriend. The conflict extends beyond the classroom, impacting other characters like Ayisha, who faces familial opposition for her faith, and Amy, who grapples with her atheism in the face of a cancer diagnosis. The film culminates in a dramatic confrontation and resolution, solidifying the centrality of conflict to the narrative's progression and thematic exploration.

title: Son of God
justification: Structural conflict is a dominant force in "The Word Became Flesh." The narrative is propelled by the escalating antagonism between Jesus and the Jewish authorities, particularly the Pharisees and High Priest Caiaphas. This conflict is evident in dialogues such as the Pharisees accusing Jesus of blasphemy ("Isn't that blasphemy?") and plotting against him ("This cannot continue. He ridicules our laws...insults the traditions of our fathers."). The Roman occupation adds another layer of conflict, with figures like Pontius Pilate struggling to maintain order amidst the growing unrest caused by Jesus's followers and the threat of rebellion ("Disorder will not be tolerated."). The film culminates in Jesus's arrest, trial, and crucifixion, driven by the sustained opposition from both religious and political powers, making conflict the central engine of the story.

title: Planes: Fire and Rescue
justification: Structural conflict is a central engine driving the narrative. The initial conflict arises from Dusty's failing gearbox, threatening his racing career. This leads to a new conflict: saving Propwash Junction by becoming a firefighter, which involves overcoming challenges in training and facing dangerous wildfires. The film escalates tension with the threat of the Fusel Lodge fire and Blade Ranger's injury, forcing Dusty to confront his limitations and fears. The climax involves a high-stakes rescue mission, solidifying conflict as a dominant force shaping character decisions and narrative progression.

title: The Grand Budapest Hotel
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The subtitles reveal a persistent antagonism between Gustave and the Desgoffe und Taxis family, escalating from a dispute over a valuable painting to accusations of murder. Gustave's arrest, imprisonment, and subsequent escape drive a significant portion of the plot, creating sustained tension. The conflict escalates further with the introduction of Jopling, a ruthless enforcer, and the outbreak of war, which directly impacts the characters' decisions and actions. The narrative is structured around these high-stakes oppositions, making conflict the central element.

title: RoboCop
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The central conflict revolves around the struggle between Omnicorp's desire to deploy robotic law enforcement and the resistance to this technology, both politically and morally. This is evident from the outset with the debate between Pat Novak, General Monroe, and Hubert Dreyfus. The creation of RoboCop intensifies this conflict, as seen in the training sequences and the ethical dilemmas faced by Dr. Norton. Furthermore, Alex Murphy's personal vendetta against Antoine Vallon and the corrupt police force adds another layer of sustained antagonism, culminating in a final confrontation where Murphy must overcome both corporate control and criminal elements.

title: Annie
justification: Structural conflict is a dominant force in "Annie." The narrative revolves around Annie's struggle against Miss Hannigan, who exploits her for financial gain and actively thwarts her attempts to find her parents. This antagonism is evident from the outset, with Hannigan's abusive behavior and the children's desire to escape her control. Will Stacks's mayoral campaign is also structured around conflict, as he faces opposition in the polls and must overcome public perception. The climax involves a kidnapping plot orchestrated by Guy Danlily, creating a high-stakes situation where Annie's safety is threatened, and Stacks must confront the conspirators to rescue her.

title: Dracula Untold
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The central conflict revolves around Vlad's desperate attempt to protect his family and kingdom from the encroaching Turkish army, led by Sultan Mehmed. This is immediately established when Hamza Bey demands 1,000 boys for the Janissary Corps, triggering Vlad's decision to seek dark power. The escalating tension is evident in Vlad's transformation, his battles against the Turks, and the constant threat to his loved ones, culminating in Mirena's death and Vlad's full embrace of his Dracula persona. The film's plot is almost entirely driven by this sustained antagonism and the high stakes involved.

title: Exodus: Gods and Kings
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The central conflict revolves around the antagonism between Moses and Ramses, and the escalating tension between the Egyptians and the enslaved Hebrews. The dialogue explicitly establishes the Hittite threat, setting the stage for military conflict. Later, the conflict escalates as Moses confronts Ramses about the treatment of the slaves, leading to direct confrontations and threats. The plagues serve as a series of escalating conflicts, culminating in the death of the firstborn and the pursuit of the fleeing Hebrews, making conflict the primary driver of the plot.

title: The Hundred-Foot Journey
justification: Structural conflict is a central engine driving the narrative. The film establishes an initial conflict through political violence in India, forcing the family to flee. This is followed by a sustained and escalating rivalry between the Kadam family's restaurant and Madame Mallory's Michelin-starred establishment, involving sabotage, competitive maneuvers, and open hostility. The conflict shapes character decisions, particularly Hassan's, as he navigates loyalty to his family and his ambition as a chef. The fire at the Kadam's restaurant marks a significant escalation, highlighting the intensity of the antagonism.

title: No Good Deed
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The film opens with news reports about Colin Evans, a convicted criminal up for parole, immediately establishing a central conflict. His parole hearing is fraught with opposition, as someone argues against his release, citing his violent tendencies. After being denied parole, Colin escapes and terrorizes Terry and her family, creating a sustained and escalating conflict. The narrative revolves around Terry's struggle to protect herself and her children from Colin, who is portrayed as a malignant narcissist with violent tendencies. The conflict escalates to a point where lives are lost, and Terry is forced to confront Colin in a final, high-stakes confrontation.

title: Horrible Bosses 2
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The central conflict revolves around three friends who are screwed over by a ruthless businessman, Bert Hanson, and his son, Rex. This antagonism escalates as the friends initially try to get their company back through legal means, but then resort to increasingly desperate and illegal schemes, including kidnapping. The dialogue is filled with threats, escalating tension, and strategic confrontations as the friends try to outwit the Hansons and reclaim what they believe is rightfully theirs. The high stakes of losing their business and livelihoods drive their decisions and actions throughout the film, making conflict the primary driver of the plot.

title: Muppets Most Wanted
justification: The film's narrative is heavily driven by structural conflict. The central conflict revolves around Constantine, the world's most dangerous frog, replacing Kermit and using the Muppets' world tour as a cover for a series of heists, culminating in the theft of the Crown Jewels. This antagonism is sustained throughout the film, creating escalating tension as Kermit is imprisoned and the Muppets are manipulated. The conflict shapes character decisions, particularly Kermit's struggle to escape and expose Constantine, and Piggy's internal conflict about her feelings. The film's plot is almost entirely propelled by this central conflict, making it a dominant structural engine.

title: Ouija
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The subtitles reveal a sustained and escalating conflict with malevolent spirits, initiated by the use of a Ouija board. The initial conflict arises from the mysterious death of Debbie, prompting Laine and her friends to use the board, against warnings, to contact her. This escalates into a direct confrontation with the spirit of Doris Zander and her mother, marked by explicit threats ('Run, she's coming'), escalating danger (possession, physical attacks), and high stakes (the deaths of multiple characters). The narrative is almost entirely driven by the characters' attempts to understand and combat these supernatural forces, making conflict the central organizing principle.

title: Jack Ryan: Shadow Recruit
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The subtitles reveal a sustained antagonism between the US and Russia, escalating from economic warfare to a planned terrorist attack and economic collapse. Dialogue such as "Then we will regard this as an act of economic war" and "America will bleed" establishes this persistent opposition. The threat of a coordinated terrorist attack and economic sabotage drives the plot, with characters like Jack Ryan actively working to prevent it, as evidenced by lines like "I think there's a coordinated plot within Russia to collapse the dollar and crash the U.S. economy." The high stakes are emphasized by the potential for "Hyperinflation. Bread lines. Rioting." and the need to stop the attack "programmed for 9:06 a.m."

title: The Boxtrolls
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The central conflict revolves around Archibald Snatcher's relentless pursuit to exterminate the boxtrolls to gain a white hat and social status, creating sustained antagonism. This is evident from Snatcher's dialogue: "I will destroy every last boxtroll in this town!" and his actions throughout the film. The town's fear of the boxtrolls, fueled by Snatcher's propaganda ("They will add your flesh to their rivers of blood, and mountains of bones."), establishes a persistent threat. The escalating tension culminates in a final confrontation where Eggs and the boxtrolls must fight back against Snatcher's extermination efforts, making conflict the primary driver of the plot.

title: If I Stay
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The inciting incident, a car accident, immediately introduces high stakes and sustained antagonism. Mia's struggle to survive and make life-altering decisions under immense pressure forms the core conflict. The dialogue emphasizes the critical nature of her condition ('If she wants to live, she better start fighting') and the gravity of her choice between life and death, love and ambition. The film revolves around her internal conflict and the external consequences of her decisions, making conflict the primary driver of the plot.

title: The Book of Life
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The central conflict revolves around a wager between La Muerte and Xibalba concerning which of two boys, Manolo and Joaquin, will marry Maria. This wager directly influences events, as Xibalba actively interferes to ensure Joaquin's success, creating escalating tension and danger. The threat of Chakal and his bandits also drives the narrative, forcing characters to make high-stakes decisions. Manolo's internal conflict between family tradition and his own desires further fuels the story, culminating in a final confrontation with Xibalba's bulls and Chakal's army.

title: About Last Night
justification: Structural conflict is a dominant force in this film. The narrative revolves around the tumultuous relationships between Danny, Debbie, Bernie, and Joan, characterized by persistent antagonism and escalating tension. The dialogue reveals recurring arguments, breakups, and reconciliations, such as the constant bickering between Bernie and Joan, and the central conflict of Danny and Debbie's relationship as they navigate commitment and personal growth. The high stakes of these relationships shape character decisions, as seen in Debbie's ultimatum to Danny about his job and their subsequent breakup. The film's progression is largely driven by these sustained confrontations, making conflict a central engine of the story.

title: Into the Storm
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The plot revolves around the escalating threat of tornadoes and the characters' struggle for survival against these destructive forces. The dialogue is replete with warnings, urgent instructions, and panicked reactions to the approaching storms, such as "Oh, shit! Tornado!" and "Get us out of here. Go!" The conflict escalates as the characters face increasingly dangerous situations, including downed power lines, blocked roads, and multiple converging tornadoes. The high stakes are evident in the characters' desperate attempts to find shelter and save each other, culminating in the loss of life and the destruction of their town. The film's narrative progression is almost entirely driven by the sustained antagonism between the characters and the tornadoes.

title: Jersey Boys
justification: Structural conflict is a central engine driving the narrative. The film portrays persistent antagonism, threats, and escalating tension, particularly through Tommy DeVito's character. The subtitles reveal his involvement in criminal activities, debts, and volatile relationships, creating sustained confrontation. The dialogue highlights the high stakes involved, such as owing money to dangerous individuals ('They want their money. Now. Before something unfortunate happens') and the constant threat of violence ('Wasn't for me, we would have wound up in the trunk with a bullet in our head.'). Frankie's decisions are often shaped by these conflicts, as seen in his attempts to help Tommy and navigate the dangerous world around him.

title: The Judge
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The central conflict revolves around Judge Palmer being accused of murder, leading to sustained antagonism between him and the prosecutor, Dwight Dickham. This conflict escalates throughout the film, shaping major developments such as the preliminary hearing, the trial, and the introduction of new evidence. The high stakes of the trial, with Judge Palmer facing imprisonment, drive character decisions and create persistent tension. The dialogue is replete with confrontational exchanges, legal arguments, and personal attacks, underscoring the centrality of the conflict to the narrative's progression.

title: Blended
justification: Structural conflict is a central engine in this film, primarily revolving around relationship dynamics and personal struggles. The narrative is driven by Lauren's attempts to navigate single motherhood, dating, and co-parenting with her ex-husband, Mark, leading to recurring conflicts. For example, Mark's unreliability and infidelity create tension, as seen when he cancels plans with the kids, prompting Lauren to seek alternative solutions. The introduction of Jim and Jen's complicated relationship adds another layer of conflict, with their initial animosity gradually evolving into something more. The film culminates in a resolution of these conflicts, with Lauren ultimately choosing to pursue a relationship with Jim, signifying a shift away from the antagonism with Mark.

title: The Giver
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The dialogue establishes a society built on the suppression of individuality and emotion to eliminate conflict, but this very suppression becomes the source of a central conflict. Jonas's training as the Receiver of Memory exposes him to the pain and beauty of the past, creating an internal conflict as he questions the values of his community. This escalates into external conflict as Jonas decides to defy the Elders and release the memories, risking the stability of the community. The Elders actively try to stop Jonas, creating a sustained antagonism that drives the plot towards a high-stakes confrontation at the Boundary of Memory.

title: Need for Speed
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The subtitles reveal a persistent antagonism between Tobey Marshall and Dino Brewster, fueled by past events and escalating into a high-stakes race. The conflict is established early with references to their rivalry and Dino's actions that led to Pete's death, for which Tobey was imprisoned. Dino places a bounty on Tobey, creating immediate danger and sustained pursuit. The De Leon race itself is a sustained confrontation, with the winner taking all, and the narrative culminates in a final showdown between Tobey and Dino, where Tobey ultimately exposes Dino's guilt, resolving the central conflict.

title: St. Vincent
justification: Structural conflict is a dominant force in this film. The narrative is propelled by several persistent antagonisms: Maggie's custody battle with her ex-husband, Vin's financial struggles and health issues, Oliver's bullying at school, and Vin's gruff exterior causing friction with nearly everyone he encounters. The threat of losing custody looms large for Maggie, shaping her decisions and creating tension. Vin's confrontations with bill collectors, hospital staff, and even Maggie herself escalate throughout the film, driving the plot forward. The film culminates in a custody hearing where the conflicts surrounding Maggie's parenting and Vin's influence come to a head.

title: John Wick
justification: The film's narrative is overwhelmingly driven by conflict. The inciting incident is the theft of John Wick's car and the killing of his dog, which sets off a chain of escalating violence. Viggo Tarasov places a contract on Wick, leading to sustained confrontations with assassins and henchmen. The dialogue emphasizes the high stakes and the persistent threat Wick faces, such as Viggo's warning: "John will come for you. And you will do nothing...because you can do nothing." The entire plot revolves around Wick's pursuit of revenge and the attempts to stop him, making conflict the central engine of the story.

title: A Million Ways to Die in The West
justification: Structural conflict is a central engine of the narrative. The film opens with a direct threat to Albert's life: "You said you would kill my family and burn my house down if l didn't, so... Draw." This sets up a high-stakes opposition that, though initially resolved, returns to structure the plot. Charlie Blanche's threat, "If l don't have that cash, l'm coming after ya," establishes a ticking clock. Later, Clinch Leatherwood's arrival escalates the conflict, with his ultimatum: "Either he meets me outside in the main thoroughfare at noon tomorrow or l start killing more people." The narrative then builds towards a final confrontation, with Albert ultimately facing Clinch in a gunfight, solidifying conflict as a primary driver.

title: Dolphin Tale 2
justification: Structural conflict is a central engine in this film, primarily revolving around the well-being of the dolphins and the aquarium's future. The core conflict arises from Winter's deteriorating condition after Panama's death, leading to potential USDA violations and the threat of Winter being moved ("That's a transfer order. They're moving Winter to a marine park... in Texas."). This threat drives character decisions, such as the risky attempt to pair Winter with Hope. Additionally, there's conflict regarding Mandy's release versus keeping her to comfort Winter, highlighting the tension between animal welfare and the aquarium's mission ("If Mandy can go home, then she deserves to go home."). The film also features institutional conflict, with the USDA inspector threatening violations and the aquarium struggling to balance rescue efforts with public entertainment.

title: The Expendables 3
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The core conflict revolves around the Expendables' mission to eliminate or capture Stonebanks, a former member turned arms dealer. This antagonism drives nearly all major plot developments, from the initial failed mission and Caesar's injury to the recruitment of a new team and the final confrontation in Azmenistan. Explicit threats and escalating tension are constant, as Stonebanks repeatedly outmaneuvers the team, captures its members, and threatens their lives. The high stakes of this opposition shape character decisions, particularly Barney's determination to confront Stonebanks despite the risks and the team's willingness to risk their lives to rescue their captured comrades.

title: Earth to Echo
justification: The film's narrative is heavily driven by conflict. The central conflict revolves around the construction company's plan to build a freeway through the protagonists' neighborhood, forcing them to move. This is evident when Tuck says, "These guys want our houses. Maybe if we expose them for illegal property, then..." This conflict escalates when the kids discover an alien, Echo, and become targets of the construction company, who are revealed to be government agents seeking to capture Echo. The conflict intensifies as the kids evade the agents, try to help Echo escape, and ultimately confront them to protect their community, as Tuck states, "This is not just about us anymore. It's about other people now, a whole community still asleep in their beds."

title: Sex Tape
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The central conflict revolves around the accidental release of a sex tape made by the main characters, Annie and Jay. This event triggers a series of escalating confrontations as they attempt to retrieve the iPads containing the video, facing opposition from various individuals who have received the video. The threat of public exposure and the potential damage to their reputations and relationships drive their decisions and actions throughout the film, creating sustained tension and shaping the narrative's progression. The conflict escalates to include blackmail, physical altercations, and strategic maneuvers, making it the primary force driving the plot.

title: August: Osage County
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The central conflict revolves around the dysfunctional Weston family, marked by persistent antagonism, escalating tension, and high-stakes opposition. Violet's pill addiction and abusive behavior create constant conflict with her daughters, as evidenced by their frequent arguments and attempts to control her. Beverly's disappearance and subsequent death trigger a series of confrontations, exposing long-held secrets and resentments. The revelation of incestuous relationships and past betrayals further intensifies the conflict, shaping character decisions and driving the narrative forward, as seen in the explosive dinner scene and Barbara's ultimate decision to leave.

title: Million Dollar Arm
justification: Structural conflict is a central theme, primarily manifested as the protagonists' struggle to establish their sports management agency and find success. The initial conflict arises when their client is poached by a larger firm, leading to financial strain and internal tension ("We just need another play. / We don't have another play, okay?"). This drives the narrative towards finding a new strategy, culminating in the 'Million Dollar Arm' contest. The conflict escalates with challenges in India, including logistical problems and cultural misunderstandings ("Vivek, I need things to run on time and smoothly, but actually run on time and smoothly, not Indian on time and smoothly."). Further conflict emerges as they face skepticism and setbacks in training the Indian athletes, culminating in a high-stakes tryout that determines their future.

title: This is Where I Leave You
justification: Structural conflict is a dominant force in this film. The narrative is driven by persistent antagonism and escalating tension between family members, particularly the three siblings, Judd, Wendy, and Phillip, as they navigate their father's death and the subsequent shiva. This is evident in their frequent arguments, revealed secrets, and unresolved past issues, such as Judd's divorce and Quinn's pregnancy, which create sustained confrontation. The conflict is further heightened by the introduction of external characters like Wade, Annie, and Tracy, who exacerbate existing tensions and create new sources of opposition. The high stakes of family relationships and personal crises shape character decisions and drive the narrative forward, making conflict a central engine of the story.

title: Paranormal Activity: The Marked Ones
justification: The film's narrative is overwhelmingly driven by escalating conflict. Initially, the conflict is subtle, with hints of unease surrounding Ana and Oscar's strange behavior. However, this quickly escalates into violence and mystery after Ana's death, with the protagonists investigating and becoming targets themselves. The dialogue reveals escalating threats, such as Arturo's gang involvement and the growing danger surrounding Jesse's possession, exemplified by lines like, "They took Jesse!" and the frantic search to save him. The film culminates in a violent confrontation at the coven's house, solidifying conflict as the central engine of the plot.

title: Nightcrawler
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The central character, Lou Bloom, relentlessly pursues increasingly dangerous and morally questionable footage, creating sustained antagonism with competitors, law enforcement, and even his own assistant. The dialogue is replete with evidence of escalating tension, threats, and high-stakes opposition, such as Lou's negotiation with Nina for footage, his interactions with Joe Loder, and his manipulation of Rick. The film culminates in a police chase and shootout, directly resulting from Lou's actions, solidifying conflict as the primary driver of the plot.

title: Chef
justification: Structural conflict is a central engine driving the narrative. The film opens with Carl facing a make-or-break review, immediately establishing high stakes. This conflict escalates as the negative review goes viral, leading to a public confrontation with the critic ("Why don't you come by again tonight? I got a whole new menu just for you, asshole."). Carl's subsequent firing and struggle to redefine his career create sustained antagonism. The conflict with Riva, his former boss, is a recurring element, and the tension surrounding Carl's professional reputation shapes his decisions throughout the film. Even his relationship with his son is initially fraught with conflict, stemming from Carl's workaholic lifestyle and perceived failures as a father.

title: 3 Days to Kill
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The central plot revolves around Ethan Renner's mission to eliminate the Wolf, a high-stakes objective set by the CIA, creating persistent antagonism. This is evident from the opening dialogue: "Your target is the Wolf. We have reason to believe he'll be present. Find him and eliminate him." The experimental drug offered by Vivi introduces escalating tension and shapes Ethan's decisions, as seen in their recurring confrontations: "In exchange for your cleaning services, I could offer you an experimental drug. Interested?" The film sustains conflict through Ethan's dangerous missions, his struggle with terminal illness, and his efforts to reconnect with his estranged daughter, all driven by the overarching threat and opposition.

title: Deliver Us from Evil
justification: The film's narrative is overwhelmingly driven by conflict. From the opening scene of sustained gunfire to the climactic exorcism, antagonism is constant. The protagonist, Sarchie, faces escalating threats, including violent disputes, a possessed woman, and a malevolent entity manipulating events. The central conflict revolves around Sarchie's investigation into supernatural occurrences, his confrontation with the demonic forces, and his desperate attempt to save his family. The dialogue is saturated with urgency, fear, and direct confrontation, highlighting the centrality of conflict to the plot's progression, making it the dominant structural engine.

title: Get on Up
justification: Structural conflict is a dominant force in the narrative. James Brown faces persistent opposition in various forms, including racial prejudice ("We did not drive all the way down to New Orleans to swim in a pool full of niggers!"), industry gatekeepers ("Negroes don't buy albums."), and internal band disputes over finances and recognition ("We asked to be paid on time."). These conflicts escalate throughout the film, shaping Brown's decisions and driving the plot forward. The film also highlights Brown's internal conflict and his struggle to maintain control and relevance in a changing world, as evidenced by his interactions with his band and his mother. The constant struggle for artistic and financial control, coupled with racial and social barriers, positions conflict as a central engine of the story.

title: When the Game Stands Tall
justification: Structural conflict is a central engine of the film, primarily manifested through the team's struggle to maintain their unprecedented winning streak and the internal and external pressures it creates. The dialogue highlights the persistent antagonism from rival teams, as seen in the league's attempt to penalize De La Salle for their success and Pittsburg High's desire to end the streak. Explicit threats and escalating tension are evident in the game against Long Beach Poly, described as the 'toughest game on their schedule.' Sustained confrontation is present in the players' internal struggles with commitment and leadership, as well as external challenges like T.K.'s death and Coach Ladouceur's heart attack, which directly shape character decisions and drive the narrative forward. The conflict surrounding the streak and the team's identity is a dominant force throughout the film.

title: Draft Day
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The entire plot revolves around the high-stakes conflict of the NFL draft, where the protagonist, Sonny Weaver Jr., faces immense pressure to make the right decisions for the Cleveland Browns. This pressure escalates due to the recent death of his father, the team's legendary coach, and threats to his job security. Sonny engages in sustained strategic confrontations with other teams, his coach, and the team owner, all while navigating personal conflicts, including an unexpected pregnancy. The central conflict is whether Sonny can overcome these obstacles and make the right choices to save football in Cleveland, driving nearly all narrative progression.

title: Oculus
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The subtitles reveal a sustained antagonism between the protagonists, Kaylie and Tim, and a supernatural entity residing within a mirror. This conflict is established early and escalates throughout the film, with Kaylie determined to prove the mirror's malevolent influence and Tim initially skeptical but eventually drawn into the confrontation. The narrative revolves around their preparations, investigations, and ultimately, their struggle against the mirror's power, with high stakes including their sanity and survival. Dialogue such as "We have to kill that thing" and Kaylie's detailed explanations of the mirror's history and their precautions underscore the centrality of this conflict.

title: Jurassic World
justification: Structural conflict is a dominant force in 'Jurassic World.' The narrative revolves around the dangers of genetically engineered dinosaurs, particularly the Indominus rex, which escapes containment and threatens the park's visitors. This threat is established early when Claire states, 'We have an asset out of containment,' and escalates as the dinosaur's intelligence and killing capabilities become apparent ('She is learning where she fits in the food chain, and I'm not sure you want her to figure that out'). The film features sustained confrontation, including military attempts to control the Indominus and the Raptors, as well as strategic decisions made by characters to survive and contain the threat, making conflict central to the plot's progression.

title: Star Wars Ep. VII: The Force Awakens
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the narrative. The film is driven by the escalating conflict between the Resistance and the First Order, with the latter posing an explicit threat to the galaxy. This antagonism shapes character decisions, such as Finn's defection and Rey's involvement. The First Order's pursuit of the map to Luke Skywalker and their use of the Starkiller Base create sustained tension and high stakes. The film culminates in a major confrontation at Starkiller Base, where the Resistance attempts to destroy the weapon, highlighting the centrality of conflict to the plot's progression.

title: Avengers: Age of Ultron
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The subtitles reveal a sustained, escalating conflict between the Avengers and Hydra, then Ultron. The initial attack on Strucker's base immediately establishes high stakes, with dialogue like "We are under attack!" and "They have to be after the sceptre." This antagonism quickly shifts to Ultron, whose stated mission is "The Avengers' extinction," creating a persistent threat. The film's progression is largely defined by the Avengers' attempts to thwart Ultron's plans, culminating in a large-scale battle in Sokovia, where the fate of the world hangs in the balance. The dialogue is replete with strategic planning, escalating tension, and direct confrontation, making conflict the central driver of the plot.

title: Inside Out
justification: Structural conflict is a central engine driving the narrative. The film establishes an initial state of harmony, but this is quickly disrupted by the move to San Francisco, which introduces immediate and escalating conflict. Riley's internal emotional turmoil, represented by the struggles within Headquarters, directly fuels her external conflicts with her parents and peers. The loss of Core Memories and the resulting instability of Riley's personality islands create a sustained antagonistic force that shapes her decisions, culminating in her decision to run away. The emotions' desperate journey to restore Riley's emotional balance is fraught with danger and escalating tension, making conflict the primary driver of the plot.

title: Furious 7
justification: The film's narrative is heavily structured around sustained conflict. The primary driver is the escalating antagonism between Dom's crew and Deckard Shaw, a British Special Forces assassin seeking revenge for his brother's defeat. This conflict manifests through explicit threats ("Anything happens to him, I'll come by looking for you."), physical confrontations (numerous fight scenes, car chases, and explosions), and strategic maneuvering (acquiring God's Eye to hunt Shaw). The high stakes are evident in the repeated near-death experiences of the characters and the loss of Han, fueling Dom's determination to stop Shaw ("He killed Han. Almost killed my family."). The narrative progresses almost entirely through this cycle of threat, retaliation, and escalation, making conflict the dominant structural engine.

title: American Sniper
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The subtitles reveal a sustained and escalating series of confrontations, primarily centered around the Iraq War. The protagonist, Chris Kyle, faces persistent antagonism from enemy forces, engaging in numerous firefights and sniper duels. The dialogue explicitly highlights the high stakes of these conflicts, with constant threats of death and injury. The narrative progresses through Kyle's multiple deployments, each marked by escalating tension and direct confrontation, culminating in his pursuit of a high-value target. The film also shows the internal conflict that Kyle faces as he struggles to return to civilian life.

title: Minions
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The Minions' central goal is to find and serve the most despicable master, which inherently involves conflict. This quest leads them to various antagonistic relationships, culminating in their service to Scarlet Overkill. The narrative escalates as they attempt to steal the Queen's crown, leading to direct confrontation with authorities and other villains. Scarlet's betrayal and subsequent attempts to eliminate the Minions further intensify the conflict, making it the primary driver of plot progression and character decisions.

title: The Hunger Games: Mockingjay - Part 2
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The subtitles are saturated with antagonism, threats, and sustained confrontation. The central conflict revolves around the rebellion against President Snow and the Capitol, with explicit threats of violence and escalating tension evident throughout the dialogue. Katniss's journey is defined by high-stakes opposition, shaping her decisions and actions at every turn, as seen in her participation in the war, her assassination attempt on Snow, and the constant danger she faces from both the Capitol and internal political machinations. The dialogue explicitly mentions battles, strategies, and the constant threat of death, solidifying conflict as the primary driver of the plot.

title: The Martian
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The initial conflict arises from the storm that strands Watney on Mars, immediately establishing a life-or-death struggle against the elements ("A storm warning. Commander, you should come inside."). This external conflict escalates as Watney faces resource scarcity and system failures ("If the oxygenator breaks, I'm gonna suffocate. If the water reclaimer breaks, I'll die of thirst."). A secondary conflict emerges as NASA grapples with the decision to rescue Watney, balancing risk and resources ("We either have a high chance of killing one person...or a low chance of killing six people."). The film culminates in a high-stakes rescue operation, fraught with technical challenges and requiring extreme measures ("We are going to deliberately breach the VAL to produce a reverse thrust."), solidifying conflict as the central driver of the plot.

title: Cinderella
justification: Structural conflict is a central engine in this narrative. The film establishes early conflict through the death of Ella's mother, followed by the introduction of a cruel stepmother and stepsisters who mistreat her, escalating her suffering and isolation. This antagonism drives much of Ella's actions and decisions, such as fleeing to the forest and later attending the ball despite being forbidden. The stepmother's manipulative schemes and the Grand Duke's political machinations further contribute to the sustained conflict, as they actively try to prevent Ella from being with the prince. The climax involves a kingdom-wide search and the stepmother's attempt to thwart Ella, highlighting the persistent opposition she faces.

title: Spectre
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The subtitles reveal a persistent antagonism between James Bond and the organization Spectre, led by Blofeld. This conflict is established early with Bond's unauthorized mission in Mexico leading to his grounding and escalating tension with his superiors. The narrative progresses through sustained confrontations, both physical (assassinations, chases) and strategic (thwarting Spectre's global surveillance plan). The high stakes are evident in the threats to Bond's life, the lives of those he cares about, and the security of the world, all of which drive his decisions and actions.

title: Mission: Impossible—Rogue Nation
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative, with sustained antagonism between Ethan Hunt's IMF team and the Syndicate. The subtitles reveal escalating tension through explicit threats ("Pursue us, you will be caught. Resist us, you will be killed.") and high-stakes opposition, as Hunt faces capture and death while trying to expose the Syndicate. The narrative is driven by recurring confrontations, both physical (chase scenes, fights) and strategic (outmaneuvering the CIA, infiltrating secure facilities). The core conflict shapes character decisions, forcing Hunt and his team to take extreme risks and make difficult choices to combat the Syndicate's global terror plots, making conflict the central driver of the plot.

title: Pitch Perfect 2
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The central conflict revolves around the Barden Bellas' suspension from competition after a disastrous performance. This leads to a sustained effort to regain their status and compete at the World Championships, facing persistent antagonism from the National A Cappella Association and their rivals, Das Sound Machine. The Bellas face escalating tension as they navigate internal conflicts, external challenges, and the high stakes of the competition, with their very existence as a group threatened if they fail. The narrative is almost entirely driven by this sustained antagonism and the escalating threat of failure.

title: Ant-Man
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The central conflict revolves around preventing Darren Cross from weaponizing the Yellowjacket technology and selling it to Hydra, which drives the plot forward. This is evident from Hank Pym's initial confrontation with Cross and his team ("Tell me that isn't what I think it is.") to the final battle where Scott Lang must stop Cross from unleashing chaos ("If you sell to these men, it's gonna be chaos."). The escalating tension and danger are sustained throughout the film, with explicit threats and high stakes shaping character decisions, such as Scott's decision to become Ant-Man to protect his daughter and the world ("It's not about saving our world. It's about saving theirs."). The film is structured around this central antagonism, with nearly all narrative progression driven by the need to thwart Cross's plans.

title: Home
justification: Structural conflict is a central engine driving the narrative. The film is initiated by the Boov's persistent antagonism with the Gorg, forcing them to flee and invade Earth, as Captain Smek states, "we are safe from our enemy, the Gorg." Oh's accidental invitation to the Gorg escalates the threat, leading to his fugitive status and the Boov's potential destruction: "You have doomed our species!" Tip's personal conflict centers on finding her abducted mother, creating high-stakes opposition against the Boov: "It's all your fault. You stole my mom!" The climax involves confronting the Gorg mothership to save Earth, solidifying conflict as the dominant structural element.

title: Hotel Transylvania 2
justification: Structural conflict is a central engine in this film, primarily revolving around the tension between Dracula's traditional monster views and the changing world. This is evident in his initial disapproval of Mavis's marriage to a human, Johnny, and his subsequent struggle to accept Dennis, his half-human grandson. The conflict escalates as Mavis considers moving to California, prompting Dracula to desperately try to force Dennis's vampire abilities to manifest. This leads to dangerous situations and ultimately a confrontation with Vlad, who embodies the old-school monster prejudice, creating a high-stakes opposition that shapes character decisions and drives the narrative forward. The climax involves a direct confrontation with Vlad's forces, solidifying conflict as a dominant structural element.

title: Fifty Shades of Grey
justification: Structural conflict is the dominant engine of the film's narrative. The central relationship between Anastasia and Christian is defined by persistent antagonism and escalating tension stemming from his dominant/submissive desires. Christian's controlling behavior and the inherent power imbalance create sustained confrontation, as evidenced by their constant arguments about the contract and his rules: "If you follow them, I'll reward you. If you don't, I'll punish you."
